Christmas foods.Mince pie: Mince pies once held minced meat along with spices and fruit, and now hold only dried fruit and suet or butter.
Christmas foods.Panettone: Panettone is a tall, dome-shaped Milanese sweet bread with candied fruit, and a good one may take days to make.
Christmas foods.Stollen: Stollen is a German fruit bread dusted with sugar, and Dresden's Christstollen is famed and has its own annual festival.
Christmas foods.Gingerbread: Gingerbread houses grew popular in Germany after the Brothers Grimm's Hansel and Gretel was published.
Christmas foods.Eggnog: Eggnog is a creamy drink of milk, eggs, and spirits, and it began in medieval Britain as a hot drink for the wealthy.
Christmas foods.Yule log: The French bûche de Noël is a sponge cake rolled up to look like a log, a nod to the old custom of burning a Yule log.
Christmas foods.Candy cane: The candy cane's hooked shape is popularly said to have originated in a German choir, as a way to quiet children.
Christmas foods.Christmas pudding: Christmas pudding is traditionally made weeks ahead, on Stir-up Sunday, and set alight with brandy before serving.
Christmas foods.Mulled wine: Mulled wine is red wine warmed with spices like cloves and cinnamon, and it is sold at Christmas markets across Europe.
Christmas foods.Fruitcake: Fruitcake keeps for months or years when soaked in alcohol, and some people say a Christmas cake improves with age.
Christmas foods.Lebkuchen: Lebkuchen are German spiced honey cakes, and Nuremberg's version has been made since the Middle Ages.
Christmas foods.Hot cross bun: Hot cross buns are for Good Friday and Easter, with a cross marking the crucifixion, not Christmas.
Christmas foods.Candy corn: Candy corn is a Halloween candy, which was first made in the 1800s with a farmer-themed look.
Christmas foods.Easter egg: Easter eggs symbolize new life and spring, and chocolate versions became popular in the 19th century.
Christmas foods.Mooncake: Mooncakes are the Mid-Autumn Festival treat in China, and the round shape symbolizes the full moon and family reunion.
Christmas foods.Matzo: Matzo is the unleavened bread eaten at Passover, recalling the Israelites' hurried exodus from Egypt.
Christmas foods.Hamantaschen: Hamantaschen are triangular filled cookies for Purim, and are named for the villain Haman in the Book of Esther.
Christmas foods.Latkes: Latkes are fried potato pancakes eaten at Hanukkah, since the oil recalls the miracle of the temple lamp.
Christmas foods.Candy apple: Candy apples are a fall-fair favorite and a Halloween treat, rather than a Christmas food.
Christmas foods.Peeps: Peeps are marshmallow chicks and bunnies sold at Easter, and they are famously used in microwave and science experiments.
Christmas foods.Zongzi: Zongzi are sticky rice dumplings wrapped in bamboo leaves and eaten at the Dragon Boat Festival, honoring the poet Qu Yuan.
Christmas foods.Pączki: Pączki are Polish filled doughnuts, eaten on Fat Thursday before Lent, not at Christmas.
Christmas foods.Tangyuan: Tangyuan are sweet glutinous rice balls served at the Lantern Festival and winter solstice, and are not a Christmas food.
Christmas foods.Colomba: Colomba di Pasqua is an Italian dove-shaped Easter cake, a spring cousin of panettone, and not a Christmas bread.

Turkish foods.Döner kebab: Döner means turning in Turkish, for the rotating spit of stacked meat. The sandwich version was popularized in Berlin in the 1970s, where it became a German staple.
Turkish foods.Baklava: Baklava layers thin phyllo, nuts, and syrup, and Gaziantep's pistachio version has EU protected status. Skilled makers can roll dough sheets nearly transparent.
Turkish foods.Lahmacun: Lahmacun is a paper-thin flatbread topped with spiced minced meat, often called Turkish pizza. Locals squeeze lemon on it, add parsley, and roll it up.
Turkish foods.Pide: Pide is a boat-shaped Turkish flatbread, folded up around fillings like cheese or meat. During Ramadan, a special round pide is baked nightly.
Turkish foods.Börek: Börek is a flaky pastry stuffed with cheese, spinach, or meat. It is eaten at breakfast and is among the most common Turkish bakery snacks.
Turkish foods.Menemen: Menemen is a Turkish breakfast of eggs scrambled with tomatoes, peppers, and often onion. Whether to include onion is a hot national debate.
Turkish foods.Turkish delight: Turkish delight, or lokum, is a gel of starch and sugar. It helped by C.S. Lewis, who made it the enchanted treat in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.
Turkish foods.Simit: Simit is a ring of bread covered in sesame seeds, sold by street vendors all over Istanbul. It is the city's classic quick breakfast, often with tea.
Turkish foods.İskender: İskender kebab is sliced döner over bread, with tomato sauce and browned butter poured over it, with yogurt. It is named for İskender Efendi from Bursa, 19th century.
Turkish foods.Köfte: Köfte are spiced meatballs, and Turkey has dozens of regional types. The Tekirdağ and İnegöl kinds are among the best known.
Turkish foods.Manti: Manti are tiny Turkish dumplings, served under yogurt and spiced butter. Traditional cooks pride themselves on fitting many in a single spoon.
Turkish foods.Ayran: Ayran is a cold, salty yogurt drink, Turkey's national beverage. It is the classic partner to kebabs, and cools the heat of spiced meat.
Turkish foods.Künefe: Künefe is a dessert of shredded dough and stretchy cheese, soaked in syrup and served hot. Hatay is its most famous home.
Turkish foods.Gözleme: Gözleme is a thin hand-rolled flatbread, filled and cooked on a griddle. It is often made by women in village stalls, and spinach and cheese is typical.
Turkish foods.Spanakopita: Spanakopita is a Greek spinach-and-feta pie in phyllo. It is Greek, not Turkish, though similar spinach börek exist in Turkey.
Turkish foods.Souvlaki: Souvlaki is Greek skewered grilled meat, usually pork. It differs from Turkish kebab in the seasoning and serving style.
Turkish foods.Gyros: Gyros is Greek meat roasted on a vertical spit, close kin to döner. The word gyros is Greek for turn, and the dish is served with tzatziki.
Turkish foods.Paella: Paella is a Spanish rice dish from Valencia, named for its wide pan. It was first made with rabbit, snails, and beans, not seafood.
Turkish foods.Tagine: Tagine is both the cone-lidded clay pot and the slow-cooked stew made in it, from Morocco. The lid returns steam to the food.
Turkish foods.Pierogi: Pierogi are Polish filled dumplings, boiled and often pan-fried. Potato and cheese is the classic filling, and they are widely eaten at Christmas.
Turkish foods.Gazpacho: Gazpacho is a cold Spanish soup from Andalusia made of raw vegetables. Tomatoes only joined the recipe after arriving from the Americas.
Turkish foods.Goulash: Goulash is a Hungarian beef-and-paprika stew that began as a shepherd's food. The word gulyás means herdsman.
Turkish foods.Couscous: Couscous is tiny steamed semolina pellets, a staple across North Africa. It is Berber in origin, and UNESCO listed the knowledge around it in 2020.
Turkish foods.Biryani: Biryani is a layered rice and meat dish from South Asia, tied to Mughal kitchens. Regional versions, like Hyderabadi, are keenly defended.

Italian pasta shapes.Penne: Penne are tubes cut diagonally like a quill pen's nib, hence the name 'pens'. The ridged kind, penne rigate, holds sauce better.
Italian pasta shapes.Fusilli: Fusilli are corkscrew spirals, their name coming from 'fuso', spindle. Their twists catch sauce in the grooves.
Italian pasta shapes.Farfalle: Farfalle means butterflies in Italian, and are also known as bow ties. They're made by pinching the centre of a small rectangle.
Italian pasta shapes.Rigatoni: Rigatoni are wide, ridged tubes, from 'rigato', meaning lined. They're a classic in Rome, in dishes like carbonara and amatriciana.
Italian pasta shapes.Orecchiette: Orecchiette, meaning little ears, are a speciality of Puglia. Cooks shape them by hand by pressing a small disk with a thumb.
Italian pasta shapes.Tagliatelle: Tagliatelle are long flat ribbons from Emilia-Romagna, and are classically served with Bolognese ragù. Fresh egg pasta gives them their golden colour.
Italian pasta shapes.Linguine: Linguine means little tongues in Italian. They're flat but thinner than fettuccine, and are classic with seafood.
Italian pasta shapes.Conchiglie: Conchiglie are shell-shaped pasta, from the Italian for shell. The large ones, conchiglioni, are stuffed with cheese and baked.
Italian pasta shapes.Pappardelle: Pappardelle are very wide ribbons, perfect with rich meat ragù. The name comes from 'pappare', to gobble up.
Italian pasta shapes.Ziti: Ziti are long tubes, a traditional wedding dish in southern Italy. Baked ziti is an Italian-American staple.
Italian pasta shapes.Lasagne: Lasagne is the plural, and the single sheet is lasagna. It's one of the oldest known pasta shapes, with versions dating back to ancient times.
Italian pasta shapes.Cavatappi: Cavatappi are corkscrew-shaped hollow tubes. In the US, they're called 'cellentani', and are common in mac and cheese.
Italian pasta shapes.Udon: Udon are thick, chewy Japanese wheat noodles. They're served hot in broth or cold with dipping sauce, not Italian.
Italian pasta shapes.Soba: Soba are Japanese noodles made of buckwheat. Eating them on New Year's Eve symbolises letting go of the old year.
Italian pasta shapes.Ramen: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup, adapted from Chinese noodles. Instant ramen was invented in 1958 by Momofuku Ando.
Italian pasta shapes.Pierogi: Pierogi are Polish dumplings filled with potato, cheese or fruit. They aren't pasta, being closer to filled dough.
Italian pasta shapes.Risotto: Risotto is creamy Italian rice, and not pasta. Its arborio rice releases starch as it is stirred.
Italian pasta shapes.Polenta: Polenta is cooked cornmeal, a northern Italian staple. It was long a peasant food, based on grain from the Americas.
Italian pasta shapes.Bruschetta: Bruschetta is grilled bread with toppings, usually pronounced 'brus-KET-ta'. It originated as a way to use stale bread.
Italian pasta shapes.Focaccia: Focaccia is a flat Italian bread, dimpled and dressed with olive oil. Liguria's version is famed for it.
Italian pasta shapes.Pho: Pho is Vietnamese noodle soup of rice noodles in broth. It's usually eaten for breakfast in Hanoi.
Italian pasta shapes.Paella: Paella is a Spanish rice dish from Valencia. It's named after the wide pan it's cooked in, and the crispy bottom is a prize.
Italian pasta shapes.Tortilla: The tortilla in Spain is a thick potato omelette. Mexico's tortillas are flatbreads of corn or wheat instead.
Italian pasta shapes.Burrata: Burrata is a fresh Italian cheese, with a mozzarella shell and creamy centre. It's cheese, not pasta, born in Puglia.

French cooking terms.Sauté: Sauté comes from the French for 'jumped', describing how food hops in a hot pan when tossed.
French cooking terms.Flambé: Flambé means 'flamed': pouring alcohol into a hot pan ignites the vapor, burning off harsh edges and leaving a caramelized sweetness.
French cooking terms.Julienne: Julienne means cutting food into thin matchstick strips, and the term appeared in French cookbooks in the 1700s.
French cooking terms.Purée: Purée is a French word for 'strained', and the technique once meant pressing food through a sieve by hand.
French cooking terms.Roux: Roux is equal parts flour and fat cooked together; the darker it's cooked, the less thickening power it has but the deeper the flavor.
French cooking terms.Mirepoix: Mirepoix is the diced onion, carrot and celery base of French cooking, usually in a 2-1-1 ratio; its name honors a French duke.
French cooking terms.Bain-marie: A bain-marie is a water bath that cooks gently, and the name is said to honor Mary the Jewess, an early alchemist.
French cooking terms.Confit: Confit, from the French for 'preserved', originally meant slowly cooking duck in its own fat so it kept for months without refrigeration.
French cooking terms.Chiffonade: Chiffonade means 'made of rags' in French, and it describes cutting leafy herbs into thin ribbons by rolling and slicing.
French cooking terms.Au gratin: Au gratin describes a dish topped with breadcrumbs or cheese and browned, and it comes from 'gratter', French for to grate.
French cooking terms.Mise en place: Mise en place means 'everything in its place', the habit of prepping and measuring all ingredients before cooking begins.
French cooking terms.Brunoise: Brunoise is a tiny, precise dice, about 3 mm across, and it's usually made by first cutting a julienne.
French cooking terms.Velouté: Velouté, 'velvety', is one of the five French mother sauces, made by thickening white stock with a roux.
French cooking terms.Al dente: Al dente is Italian for 'to the tooth', describing pasta cooked to a firm bite, so it's not a French term.
French cooking terms.Antipasto: Antipasto is Italian for 'before the meal', the starter course, and it doesn't come from French cooking.
French cooking terms.Tapas: Tapas are Spanish small plates, and one legend says a slice of bread was first placed on a drink to keep flies out, from 'tapar', to cover.
French cooking terms.Wok: A wok is a Cantonese word for a round-bottomed pan, so it's Chinese, not French, and its shape concentrates heat.
French cooking terms.Teriyaki: Teriyaki is Japanese, from 'teri' (shine) and 'yaki' (grill), and the glaze gives food its glossy finish.
French cooking terms.Barbecue: Barbecue likely comes from a Caribbean Taino word, barbacoa, for a wooden grill frame, so it has no French roots.
French cooking terms.Ketchup: Ketchup likely derives from a Hokkien word for fermented fish sauce; the early British version had no tomatoes at all.
French cooking terms.Marinara: Marinara is Italian, 'mariner's style', and a plain tomato sauce needs no roux or other French technique.
French cooking terms.Bruschetta: Bruschetta comes from the Italian 'bruscare', to roast over coals, and the word is pronounced 'brus-KET-ta'.
French cooking terms.Dim sum: Dim sum is a Cantonese term, perhaps meaning 'touch the heart', so it isn't French.
French cooking terms.Sriracha: Sriracha is named for Si Racha, a coastal town in Thailand, and it's a Thai chili sauce, not a French one.

Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Spaghetti bolognese: Slippery strands flick tomato-meat sauce on its way to your mouth. Tomato stains are notoriously hard to lift from cotton.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Curry: Turmeric is a powerful natural dye and yellow stains can linger. Sunlight can bleach it out, funnily enough.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Beetroot: Its red pigment, betalain, is so strong it is used as a food dye. It also turns urine pink in some people.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Blueberries: A burst berry leaves a deep purple stain. The pigments are anthocyanins, which are also used in natural dyes.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Red wine: The classic stain. Pouring white wine or salt on a spill is a common remedy, though quick blotting is the only one that helps.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Ketchup: The tomato and vinegar combination clings and stains. A sneaky fact is that the bottle's contents come out in a burst after a pause.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Soy sauce: Thin, salty, dark liquid that soaks through cotton fast. It leaves a brown mark.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Barbecue ribs: Sticky sauce, sugary and smoky, plus finger licking. They are the messiest meal of the lot.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Pomegranate: Its juice stains deeply and was once used as a dye. Opening one underwater avoids the squirt.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Tomato soup: A hot, thin liquid that can splash on a spoon trip. Tomato's lycopene is a pigment that clings to fabric.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Coffee: Tannins in coffee leave brown stains that set as they dry. Treat it fast with cold water.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Chili dog: Chili, mustard and a dog in a bun, a drip-prone combination. Mustard also stains with turmeric.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Crackers: Dry and crumbly, so they create crumbs but no stains. A white shirt is safe.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.White rice: Plain and pale, it leaves no color behind. It is one of the safest foods for white clothes.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Popcorn: Dry, without sauce, so it is stain-free unless buttered. Butter leaves grease spots, though.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Rice cake: Dry and colorless, so it leaves no mark.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Water: Colorless and it leaves no permanent stain. At worst it dries to nothing, though hard water can leave rings.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Cucumber: Pale green and watery, with almost no pigment to stain. It is about 95 percent water.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Marshmallow: White and sticky, but invisible on a white shirt. Originally made from the root of the marshmallow plant.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Celery: Pale green and about 95 percent water, so it has too little pigment to leave a mark.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Pretzel: A dry baked snack with salt, which does not stain. Crumbs brush right off.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.White bread: Pale and dry, so it leaves little but crumbs. It is a safe pick for a white shirt.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Saltines: Plain, dry crackers that stain nothing. Their name is about the salt sprinkled on top.
Foods dangerous to eat in a white shirt.Plain bagel: Dry and pale, safe unless you add cream cheese or jam. Bagels are boiled before baking.

Canadian provinces and territories.Ontario: Home to Ottawa, Toronto, and Niagara Falls, it holds about 40 percent of Canada's population, and its name comes from an Iroquoian word for sparkling water.
Canadian provinces and territories.Quebec: The only province with French as its sole official language, it is also home to Montreal and the maple syrup that Canada is known for.
Canadian provinces and territories.British Columbia: It is the westernmost province, known for the Rockies, Vancouver, and Pacific old-growth rainforest.
Canadian provinces and territories.Alberta: Banff and Lake Louise draw visitors, and the oil sands near Fort McMurray hold some of the world's largest reserves.
Canadian provinces and territories.Manitoba: Winnipeg's black bear inspired Winnie the Pooh, and Churchill, on Hudson Bay, is known as the polar bear capital of the world.
Canadian provinces and territories.Saskatchewan: Known for wheat fields stretching to the horizon, it produces a huge share of Canada's grain, and its name comes from a Cree word for fast-flowing river.
Canadian provinces and territories.Nova Scotia: Its name is Latin for New Scotland, and the Bay of Fundy next door has some of the highest tides on Earth.
Canadian provinces and territories.New Brunswick: The only officially bilingual province, with English and French, it is home to the Hopewell Rocks, flowerpot formations at the Fundy shore.
Canadian provinces and territories.Prince Edward Island: Canada's smallest province is the setting of Anne of Green Gables, and it is linked to the mainland by the 13-kilometer Confederation Bridge.
Canadian provinces and territories.Yukon: The Klondike Gold Rush of 1896 drew about 100,000 prospectors to this northwestern territory, and it has Canada's highest peak, Mount Logan.
Canadian provinces and territories.Nunavut: Created in 1999 as Canada's newest and largest territory, its name means our land in Inuktitut, and it is home to a mainly Inuit population.
Canadian provinces and territories.Alaska: Trap: it is a US state, purchased from Russia in 1867 for about 7.2 million dollars, and it borders Yukon.
Canadian provinces and territories.Greenland: Trap: it is a self-governing territory of Denmark, the world's largest island, and is not part of Canada.
Canadian provinces and territories.New England: Trap: a region of the northeastern United States, not part of Canada, although it neighbors Quebec and New Brunswick.
Canadian provinces and territories.Maine: Trap: this US state borders both Quebec and New Brunswick but is not Canadian.
Canadian provinces and territories.Vermont: Trap: a US state that borders Quebec, and it is one of the few that joined the Union after being its own republic.
Canadian provinces and territories.Minnesota: Trap: it borders Ontario and Manitoba, and the Northwest Angle is the only part of the lower 48 north of the 49th parallel.
Canadian provinces and territories.Oregon: Trap: a US state to the south of Washington; it never touches Canada.
Canadian provinces and territories.Tasmania: Trap: an Australian island state, home to the Tasmanian devil, and nowhere near Canada.
Canadian provinces and territories.Queensland: Trap: an Australian state in the northeast, with the Great Barrier Reef off its coast.
Canadian provinces and territories.New Hampshire: Trap: a US state bordering Quebec, whose motto is Live Free or Die.
Canadian provinces and territories.Montana: Trap: a US state that borders Alberta, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia, but is American.
Canadian provinces and territories.Idaho: Trap: a US state that shares a short border with British Columbia, and is home to potatoes.
Canadian provinces and territories.New South Wales: Trap: Australia's most populous state, which contains Sydney, and it has nothing to do with Canada.

Countries in Southeast Asia.Thailand: The only Southeast Asian country never colonized by a European power, and its capital's ceremonial name is among the longest place names in the world.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Vietnam: Its capital Hanoi has a Temple of Literature dating from 1070 that is often called the country's first university.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Cambodia: Angkor Wat, built in the 12th century, is the largest religious monument on Earth, and appears on the flag.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Laos: The old kingdom here was Lan Xang, the land of a million elephants, and the Mekong forms much of the western border.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Myanmar: Also called Burma, it is home to over 2,000 temples at Bagan, many dating from the 11th to 13th centuries.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Malaysia: It is split by the South China Sea into a peninsula and part of Borneo, and the Petronas Towers were the tallest buildings in the world for six years.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Singapore: This island city-state is one of the world's most densely populated countries, and chewing gum sales are heavily restricted.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Indonesia: With over 17,000 islands, it is the world's biggest archipelago nation, and it has more active volcanoes than any other country.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Philippines: The archipelago is named for King Philip II of Spain, and it has more than 7,000 islands.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Brunei: A small, oil-rich sultanate on Borneo, the country's Sultan has one of the world's largest palaces, with about 1,700 rooms.
Countries in Southeast Asia.East Timor: Also called Timor-Leste, it became independent in 2002, and it was the first new sovereign state of the 21st century.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Bangladesh: Trap: it is in South Asia, bordered by India and Myanmar, so it is not Southeast Asian despite being adjacent.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Sri Lanka: Trap: an island nation south of India, and part of South Asia.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Nepal: Trap: in South Asia, home to Everest, and it sits in the Himalaya rather than Southeast Asia.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Bhutan: Trap: a South Asian Himalayan kingdom known for measuring Gross National Happiness.
Countries in Southeast Asia.India: Trap: South Asia, though its Andaman and Nicobar islands lie close to Myanmar and Indonesia.
Countries in Southeast Asia.China: Trap: East Asia, though it shares borders with Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar.
Countries in Southeast Asia.South Korea: Trap: it is in East Asia, and its pop culture is a global phenomenon.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Japan: Trap: East Asia, and the Japanese archipelago lies well to the north of Southeast Asia.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Mongolia: Trap: East Asia, landlocked between Russia and China.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Maldives: Trap: South Asia's island nation in the Indian Ocean, and the lowest country on Earth.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Papua New Guinea: Trap: it is classed as Oceania, even though it shares the island of New Guinea with Indonesia.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Pakistan: Trap: South Asia, and the Indus River runs the length of the country.
Countries in Southeast Asia.Afghanistan: Trap: it is in South and Central Asia, and it is landlocked.

Cities on the Nile.Cairo: Egypt's capital sits at the head of the Nile Delta, and Greater Cairo holds over 20 million people. It's the largest city in the Arab world.
Cities on the Nile.Khartoum: Sudan's capital sits where the Blue Nile meets the White Nile. The two join into one Nile, though the blue runs more muddy in flood.
Cities on the Nile.Aswan: The city in southern Egypt is near the first cataract. Its high dam created Lake Nasser, and the ancient Greeks measured Earth's size from here.
Cities on the Nile.Luxor: Ancient Thebes stood here on the Nile, and the Valley of the Kings lies across the river. It's often called the world's greatest open-air museum.
Cities on the Nile.Juba: South Sudan's capital lies on the White Nile. It became the capital of the world's newest country when South Sudan became independent in 2011.
Cities on the Nile.Jinja: The Ugandan town sits where the Nile leaves Lake Victoria. John Hanning Speke named it the source of the Nile in 1858.
Cities on the Nile.Giza: This city on the Nile's west bank is home to the Great Pyramid, built for Khufu about 4,500 years ago. It's the only Wonder of the ancient world still standing.
Cities on the Nile.Omdurman: Sudan's largest city sits across the Nile from Khartoum. In 1898, a British force won a decisive battle here against the Mahdist state.
Cities on the Nile.Dongola: A city on the Nile in northern Sudan. It's a trading center near the old Nubian kingdom of Makuria, whose capital was Old Dongola.
Cities on the Nile.Alexandria: Egypt's second city sits on the Mediterranean, west of the Nile delta. Its ancient library and lighthouse have made it famous, but the Nile's main flow doesn't pass it.
Cities on the Nile.Addis Ababa: Ethiopia's capital is on the highlands where the Blue Nile starts, but not on the Nile itself. The river begins at Lake Tana, hundreds of kilometers away.
Cities on the Nile.Nairobi: Kenya's capital lies on the Nairobi river, in the Athi basin, which drains to the Indian Ocean. It is not on the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Tripoli: The Libyan capital lies on the Mediterranean coast, nowhere near the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Port Said: This port sits at the Mediterranean end of the Suez Canal. The Nile's distributaries are well to its west.
Cities on the Nile.Jerusalem: The holy city lies in the Judean hills, far from the Nile, near the Jordan river valley.
Cities on the Nile.Baghdad: Iraq's capital lies on the Tigris river. It is not on the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Tunis: Tunisia's capital stands by the Mediterranean, and not on any big river, far from the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Mombasa: The Kenyan port is on the Indian Ocean. The Nile is thousands of kilometers inland and to the northwest.
Cities on the Nile.Riyadh: The Saudi capital is in the middle of a desert plateau, with no major river nearby.
Cities on the Nile.Kinshasa: The capital of DR Congo sits on the Congo river, which belongs to a different great river system from the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Lagos: Nigeria's biggest city is on the Atlantic coast, in the Niger's region, far from the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Mecca: This holy city lies in a dry valley in Saudi Arabia, with no river anywhere near.
Cities on the Nile.Suez: The city sits on the Red Sea end of the Suez Canal, not on the Nile.
Cities on the Nile.Damascus: Syria's capital lies on the Barada river, in an oasis, and not on the Nile.

Landmarks in India.Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan built this white marble tomb in Agra for his wife Mumtaz Mahal; it took about two decades and thousands of artisans.
Landmarks in India.Red Fort: The Mughal fortress in Delhi, in red sandstone, is where India's prime minister raises the flag every Independence Day.
Landmarks in India.Qutub Minar: Delhi's 73-metre minaret from around 1200 is the world's tallest brick minaret, and a nearby iron pillar has barely rusted in 1,500 years.
Landmarks in India.Gateway of India: Mumbai's basalt arch on the waterfront was built to mark the 1911 visit of King George V, and the last British troops left through it in 1948.
Landmarks in India.Golden Temple: Amritsar's Harmandir Sahib, holiest shrine of Sikhism, is gilded in gold and its free kitchen serves tens of thousands of meals daily.
Landmarks in India.Hawa Mahal: Jaipur's Palace of Winds has 953 small windows, built so royal women could watch street life unseen.
Landmarks in India.Varanasi: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities, on the Ganges, where pilgrims bathe at dawn on the riverside ghats.
Landmarks in India.Amber Fort: A hilltop fort near Jaipur combining Hindu and Mughal styles, with a Mirror Palace, and visitors once rode elephants up.
Landmarks in India.Lotus Temple: Delhi's Bahá'í House of Worship has 27 marble petals, and it welcomes people of all faiths and has no idols.
Landmarks in India.India Gate: Delhi's 42-metre war memorial commemorates around 70,000 Indian soldiers who died in World War I and carries thousands of their names.
Landmarks in India.Ajanta Caves: Buddhist caves carved into a cliff in Maharashtra, with paintings about 2,000 years old, lost for centuries until a British hunting party found them in 1819.
Landmarks in India.Goa: Once a Portuguese colony for over 450 years until 1961, now a beach state known for Indo-Portuguese churches.
Landmarks in India.Badshahi Mosque: A Mughal giant in Lahore, Pakistan, built in 1673, which could hold tens of thousands of worshippers.
Landmarks in India.Sigiriya: A 5th-century rock fortress in Sri Lanka rising about 200 metres, with ancient frescoes of celestial maidens.
Landmarks in India.Mount Everest: The world's highest peak sits on the border of Nepal and Tibet, so it lies outside India.
Landmarks in India.Boudhanath: Kathmandu's huge Buddhist stupa in Nepal, one of the largest in the world, with the eyes of the Buddha painted on it.
Landmarks in India.Angkor Wat: Cambodia's immense Khmer temple, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu, so a link with India but not located there.
Landmarks in India.Shwedagon Pagoda: Myanmar's gilded stupa in Yangon, covered in tonnes of gold, with a spire set with thousands of diamonds.
Landmarks in India.Petra: Jordan's rose-red city carved into the rock by the Nabataeans, reached through a narrow canyon called the Siq.
Landmarks in India.Persepolis: The ceremonial capital of ancient Persia in Iran, burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC.
Landmarks in India.Kathmandu: The capital of Nepal in a valley of seven UNESCO sites, and a gateway to the Himalayas.
Landmarks in India.Bhaktapur: A medieval city of Nepal near Kathmandu, known for its Newar woodcarving and pottery square.
Landmarks in India.Tiger's Nest: Bhutan's cliffside monastery, Paro Taktsang, clings to rock about 900 metres above the valley.

Countries with exactly 4 letters.Cuba: The largest island in the Caribbean, and its name has four letters like Peru.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Fiji: An archipelago of more than 300 islands in the Pacific, with a four-letter name.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Iran: Its name means land of the Aryans, and it was known as Persia in much of the West until 1935.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Iraq: Home of ancient Mesopotamia, often called the cradle of civilization, with a four-letter name.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Laos: A landlocked country in Southeast Asia, once known as the Land of a Million Elephants.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Mali: Its city of Timbuktu was a medieval centre of learning, and Mansa Musa may have been the richest person ever.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Oman: A Gulf sultanate famous for frankincense, which has been traded for thousands of years.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Peru: Home of Machu Picchu and the Inca Empire, with a four-letter name.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Togo: A narrow strip of West Africa, only about 50 kilometres wide in places.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Haiti: It has five letters, so it falls out, though it was the first Black republic, founded in 1804.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Nepal: Home to Mount Everest, but with five letters, so it doesn't fit.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Spain: Five letters, so not a four-letter country.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Italy: Five letters, so out, though it has 'only' four letters in its Italian name, Italia, which has six.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Yemen: Five letters, so it misses. Its capital Sanaa is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities, famed for tower houses.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Benin: Five letters, so out. The former Kingdom of Dahomey took the name Benin in 1975, borrowed from the bight, not the old Benin Empire.

Countries with exactly 4 letters.Gabon: Five letters. The name comes from the Portuguese gabão, a coat, because the Komo estuary looked like a hooded cloak.
Countries with exactly 4 letters.Guam: A four-letter name, but it is a US territory rather than a country.

Elements named after scientists.Einsteinium: Element 99 was found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952, and named for Albert Einstein, who died a few years later.
Elements named after scientists.Curium: Named for Marie and Pierre Curie, element 96 is radioactive and glows faintly in the dark. It was made in 1944 by bombarding plutonium.
Elements named after scientists.Nobelium: Element 102 honors Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite and founded the Nobel Prizes. Its discovery claim was disputed for years.
Elements named after scientists.Mendelevium: Element 101 honors Dmitri Mendeleev, who devised the periodic table. It was first made one atom at a time.
Elements named after scientists.Fermium: Honoring Enrico Fermi, builder of the first nuclear reactor, element 100 was first detected in fallout from a 1952 hydrogen bomb test.
Elements named after scientists.Rutherfordium: Element 104 honors Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus. It exists only in labs and survives mere seconds.
Elements named after scientists.Seaborgium: Element 106 honors Glenn Seaborg, who was alive when it was named in 1997, a rare honor. He co-discovered many elements.
Elements named after scientists.Bohrium: Element 107 honors Niels Bohr, who modeled how electrons orbit the nucleus. Only a few atoms of it have ever been made.
Elements named after scientists.Copernicium: Element 112 honors Nicolaus Copernicus, who placed the Sun at the center of the solar system. It was named on his birthday in 2010.
Elements named after scientists.Meitnerium: Element 109 honors Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission yet was overlooked for the Nobel Prize her colleague received.
Elements named after scientists.Lawrencium: Element 103 honors Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, the particle accelerator that made so many new elements possible.
Elements named after scientists.Americium: A trap: it's named for the continent, not a person. A tiny amount sits inside most household smoke detectors.
Elements named after scientists.Francium: A trap: it's named for France, not a scientist. It is so rare that less than a few dozen grams exist in Earth's crust at any time.
Elements named after scientists.Polonium: A trap: Marie Curie named it for her homeland Poland, not a scientist. It was the poison used to kill Alexander Litvinenko in 2006.
Elements named after scientists.Germanium: A trap: named for Germany, not a person. It was used in the first transistors before silicon took over.
Elements named after scientists.Californium: A trap: named for California and its university, not a scientist. A speck of it is a strong neutron source.
Elements named after scientists.Plutonium: A trap: named after the dwarf planet Pluto, not a person. It powers some space probes, like those on Mars rovers and Voyager.
Elements named after scientists.Neptunium: A trap: it's named for the planet Neptune, not a scientist. It was the first element heavier than uranium ever found.
Elements named after scientists.Uranium: A trap: named for the planet Uranus, not a scientist. Martin Klaproth discovered it in 1789.
Elements named after scientists.Helium: A trap: from Greek helios, the Sun. It was detected in sunlight before being found on Earth, so no scientist's name appears.
Elements named after scientists.Titanium: A trap: it's named for the Titans of Greek myth, not a scientist. It is as strong as steel but far lighter, popular in jets and implants.
Elements named after scientists.Thorium: A trap: it honors Thor, the Norse god of thunder, not a scientist. Some future reactors might use it as a fuel.
Elements named after scientists.Promethium: A trap: named for the Titan Prometheus who stole fire, not a scientist. It is radioactive and glows pale blue.
Elements named after scientists.Osmium: A trap: from Greek osme, meaning smell, for its pungent oxide. It is the densest naturally occurring element.

Astronomers.Galileo Galilei: He was first to publish telescope views of Jupiter's moons and the Moon's craters, and he was tried by the Inquisition for backing Copernicus.
Astronomers.Nicolaus Copernicus: His 1543 book put the Sun, not Earth, at the center of the known universe. He reportedly saw a printed copy only on his deathbed.
Astronomers.Johannes Kepler: He discovered that planets move in ellipses rather than circles, and he did it using another astronomer's superb observations.
Astronomers.Edwin Hubble: The Hubble Space Telescope is named for him. In the 1920s he showed that other galaxies exist and that they're moving away from us.
Astronomers.Carl Sagan: He made astronomy famous on TV with Cosmos, helped design the Pioneer plaques and Voyager's Golden Record, and championed the search for life.
Astronomers.Tycho Brahe: The Danish astronomer lost part of his nose in a duel and wore a metal replacement. His naked-eye measurements were the best of his time.
Astronomers.Edmond Halley: He predicted that a comet seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 would return in 1758. It did, after his death, and carries his name.
Astronomers.William Herschel: He discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope, and also found infrared light.
Astronomers.Ptolemy: The Greek-Egyptian astronomer's Earth-centered model of the cosmos was the standard for about 1,400 years.
Astronomers.Vera Rubin: Her galaxy-rotation measurements showed stars at the edges spin too fast for the visible matter, which was key evidence for dark matter.
Astronomers.Henrietta Leavitt: She discovered that a certain kind of pulsating star has a brightness tied to its period, giving astronomers a way to measure cosmic distances.
Astronomers.Clyde Tombaugh: A young Kansas farm worker who found Pluto in 1930 while comparing photographic plates, and who later discovered hundreds of asteroids.
Astronomers.Caroline Herschel: William's sister and a fine astronomer in her own right, she discovered several comets and was the first woman paid for scientific work in England.
Astronomers.Charles Darwin: He's the one who first turned a telescope on Jupiter and its moons. Wait, he's here as the starter of telescopic astronomy.
Astronomers.Gregor Mendel: Darwin studied living things, from barnacles to finches, so he is a biologist rather than an astronomer.
Astronomers.Louis Pasteur: A monk who discovered the laws of heredity using pea plants, not the sky.
Astronomers.Alexander Fleming: A French chemist who proved that microbes spoil milk and wine, and developed a rabies vaccine.
Astronomers.Antoine Lavoisier: A Scottish bacteriologist who found penicillin by noticing mold killing bacteria on a dish.
Astronomers.Dmitri Mendeleev: The father of modern chemistry, who named oxygen and hydrogen and wrote down the conservation of mass.
Astronomers.Sigmund Freud: A Russian chemist whose periodic table predicted elements before they were found.
Astronomers.Thomas Edison: The founder of psychoanalysis, who studied the mind and dreams rather than the stars.
Astronomers.Guglielmo Marconi: An American inventor of the phonograph and a long-lasting light bulb, with over a thousand patents.
Astronomers.Alan Turing: The Italian who sent wireless radio signals across the Atlantic in 1901, an engineer rather than an astronomer.
Astronomers.Florence Nightingale: The British mathematician who broke Enigma codes and laid foundations for computer science.

Things that rely on refraction of light.Rainbow: Each raindrop bends and reflects sunlight, sending violet back at about 40 degrees and red at 42; every observer sees a personal rainbow.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Mirage: Hot air near the ground bends light upward, so the shimmering road 'water' is actually a refracted image of the sky.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Sun halo: The 22-degree ring around the Sun is sunlight bending through hexagonal ice crystals in high, thin cirrus cloud.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Bent straw in water: Light slows in water and bends at the surface, so the straw seems broken even though only your view of it is.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Twinkling stars: Starlight bends through shifting pockets of air, so each star flickers; planets, seen as tiny disks rather than points, twinkle far less.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Sun dog: These bright spots beside the Sun come from flat ice crystals bending light by 22 degrees; their formal name is parhelia.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Prism spectrum: Newton showed in the 1660s that white light splits into colours inside glass, and that a second prism can recombine them.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Eyeglasses: Lenses bend light to correct the focus of your eye, and the first wearable spectacles appeared in Italy around the 1280s.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Camera lens: Glass elements bend light onto the sensor, and modern lenses stack a dozen or more so that colours do not fringe.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Echo: A trap: an echo is sound reflecting off a surface, and you need a wall roughly 17 metres away to hear it as separate.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Aurora: Charged particles from the Sun excite gases high in the atmosphere, which then emit light themselves; nothing is bent.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Shadow: A shadow is just light blocked while travelling in straight lines, which is the opposite of bending.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Solar eclipse: The Moon blocks the Sun through pure geometry; it is about 400 times smaller yet 400 times closer, so the disks nearly match.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Lightning: A bolt heats air to around 30,000 degrees Celsius, hotter than the Sun's surface, and the glow is emission, not bending.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Static shock: Electrons jump between charged surfaces; this is electricity, and no light is being bent anywhere.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Moon phases: Phases come from how much of the Moon's sunlit half we see as it orbits; Earth's shadow is not involved, a common mix-up.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Thunder: It is the sound of air expanding explosively around a lightning bolt, so refraction of light is not involved.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Tides: They come from the gravity of the Moon and Sun pulling on the oceans; light bending has nothing to do with them.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Magnetism: A force created by moving electric charge, and it is why a compass needle points north; it is not an optical effect.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Seasons: They come from Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt, not distance; Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Blue sky: A trap: the sky is blue because air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths more strongly, which is scattering, not refraction.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Glow-in-the-dark: Phosphorescent materials absorb light and re-emit it slowly; that is emission, not bending.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Mirror image: A mirror reflects rather than refracts, and it flips front to back, not left to right.
Things that rely on refraction of light.Ocean waves: Water waves do bend toward shore as they slow in shallow water, which is why they arrive nearly parallel to the beach, but that is not light.

Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Lightning bolt: Lightning heats the air to about 30,000 C, roughly five times hotter than the Sun's surface, in a flash lasting microseconds.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Sun's core: The core burns near 15 million C. Sunlight takes thousands of years to random-walk out, then just 8 minutes to reach us.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Solar corona: Oddly, the corona above the Sun's surface is millions of degrees, far hotter than the surface itself. Why is still debated.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Supernova: A supernova can briefly outshine its whole galaxy, with core temperatures reaching billions of degrees.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Nuclear explosion: A fission or fusion blast reaches tens of millions of degrees in an instant, briefly hotter than the Sun's core.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Tokamak plasma: Inside a tokamak, plasma is heated to over 100 million C, hotter than the Sun's core, yet held in place by magnetic fields.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Neutron star: Newborn neutron stars start near a trillion degrees, then cool quickly. A teaspoon of one would weigh billions of tons.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Blue giant star: Blue giants burn at 20,000 C or more at the surface, several times hotter than our Sun, and live only a few million years.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Sirius: Sirius, the brightest night star, has a surface near 9,900 C, almost double our Sun's, and is only about 8.6 light-years away.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.The Big Bang: In its first second the universe was hotter than anything since, with temperatures far beyond trillions of degrees.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Lava: Erupting lava reaches about 700 to 1,200 C. Scorching, but still cooler than the Sun's roughly 5,500 C surface.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Candle flame: A candle flame's hottest zone is about 1,400 C. The bright yellow part is actually cooler, full of glowing soot.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Bunsen flame: A Bunsen burner with the air hole open reaches roughly 1,500 C, a pale blue flame still far cooler than the Sun.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Molten iron: Iron melts at about 1,540 C. Impressive for a metal, yet the Sun's surface is more than three times hotter.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Venus surface: Venus is the hottest planet, about 465 C at the surface, hot enough to melt lead but nowhere near the Sun.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Pizza oven: Wood-fired pizza ovens run around 450 to 480 C, cooking a pie in about 90 seconds, yet far from solar heat.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Blowtorch: A welding or cutting torch can top 3,000 C, hot enough to slice steel, but the Sun's surface is still hotter.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Planet Mercury: Mercury is closest to the Sun, with daytime highs near 430 C. Its nights drop to about minus 180 C, with no air to hold heat.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Red dwarf star: Red dwarfs, the most common stars, have surfaces of only about 2,500 to 3,500 C, much cooler than the Sun.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Campfire: A campfire flame is around 600 to 1,000 C, hot enough to cook, but a fraction of the Sun's surface heat.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Rocket exhaust: Rocket exhaust reaches about 3,000 C, hot enough to need special cooling, but it still falls short of the Sun's surface.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Shuttle reentry: The shuttle's heat shield endured about 1,650 C on reentry. Tough, but cooler than the Sun's roughly 5,500 C surface.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Forest fire: Wildfires reach roughly 800 to 1,200 C. They can be devastating, yet the Sun's surface is still four or five times hotter.
Hotter than the surface of the Sun.Toaster: A toaster's coils glow at only about 700 to 1,000 C, nothing close to the Sun's surface heat.

Musicians famous for playing piano.Little Richard: His pounding, standing-up piano on Tutti Frutti helped shape rock and roll, and he played with a wild energy few matched.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Jerry Lee Lewis: Nicknamed The Killer, he played standing, kicked the stool away and once set a piano on fire during Great Balls of Fire.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Fats Domino: The New Orleans star's rolling piano powered Blueberry Hill and Ain't That a Shame, among rock and roll's earliest hits.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Lang Lang: The Chinese virtuoso played at the opening of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, and began playing as a toddler.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Stevie Wonder: Signed to Motown as a child prodigy, he plays piano, harmonica and drums, and made keyboards and synthesizers a big part of his sound.

Musicians famous for playing piano.Eric Clapton: Known as Slowhand, he is a guitarist; his piano-playing friends included Elton John, but he stuck to six strings.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Keith Moon: The Who's drummer smashed kits and was famed for wild playing, not keyboard work.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Brian May: Queen's guitarist, who built his own guitar with his father. Freddie Mercury was the band's pianist.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Kurt Cobain: Nirvana's singer and guitarist is a trap only if you think of grunge; he did not play piano as his main instrument.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Louis Armstrong: A guitar hero from Mexico whose singing guitar tone is famous on Black Magic Woman. Not a pianist.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Miles Davis: The trumpeter sang with a gravelly voice and charmed the world, but he's a horn player, not a pianist.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Kenny G: The trumpeter changed jazz repeatedly, from cool jazz to fusion, though he did not play piano as his main instrument.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Yo-Yo Ma: A saxophonist who held a note for over 45 minutes with circular breathing, a Guinness record.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Carlos Santana: The cellist plays a bowed string instrument and has recorded with everyone from Bach to bluegrass players.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Charlie Parker: A famed alto saxophonist nicknamed Bird, who co-created bebop in the 1940s.
Musicians famous for playing piano.Bob Marley: The reggae legend sang and played guitar, and his album Exodus was named by Time magazine the best of the century.

Instruments usually played with a bow.Violin: A bow is strung with horsehair, rubbed with rosin so it grips the strings, and a good bow can cost as much as a car.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Viola: The viola is a little larger than the violin and tuned a fifth lower, with a deeper, warmer sound.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Cello: Cellists hold the instrument between the knees, and its spike on the floor was added in the 19th century.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Double bass: The double bass is the largest instrument in the string family, and a bass bow can be shaped German or French style.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Fiddle: Fiddle and violin are the same instrument; the difference is about style, such as bluegrass or Irish tunes.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Erhu: The erhu has two strings, and its bow hair is threaded between them, so it can never be removed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Viola da gamba: The viola da gamba is held between the legs, and has frets, unlike the modern cello that replaced it.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Sarangi: The sarangi is an Indian bowed instrument, and its sound is said to be closest to the human voice.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Musical saw: A saw bent into an S-shape and played with a bow produces an eerie, singing tone, as in classic sci-fi films.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Guitar: Trap: guitars are normally plucked or strummed, though Jimmy Page famously used a violin bow on his.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Harp: Trap: harps are plucked with the fingers, not bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Banjo: Trap: banjos are plucked or strummed, so a bow isn't usual.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Ukulele: Trap: ukuleles are strummed with the fingers, not bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Mandolin: Trap: mandolins are played with a pick, rapidly strumming each note to sustain it.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Sitar: Trap: a sitar is plucked with a wire plectrum worn on a finger, not bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Piano: Trap: piano strings are struck by hammers, not bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Harpsichord: Trap: harpsichord strings are plucked by quills, not bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Lute: Trap: the lute is plucked with the fingers.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Balalaika: Trap: a balalaika is strummed or plucked and is not bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Zither: Trap: a zither is plucked or struck, and not usually bowed.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Koto: Trap: the koto is plucked using finger picks.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Bouzouki: Trap: the bouzouki is plucked with a plectrum.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Lyre: Trap: the lyre is plucked, and it is associated with the Greek god Apollo.
Instruments usually played with a bow.Autoharp: Trap: the autoharp is strummed with chord bars, not bowed.

Musical duos.Pet Shop Boys: Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe, named after friends who worked in a pet shop.

Musical duos.Sonny & Cher: I Got You Babe, 1965, made them stars, and they later had a TV variety show.

Musical duos.The Supremes: Diana Ross, Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard, a trio.
Musical duos.Muse: Matt Bellamy, Chris Wolstenholme and Dominic Howard, a trio from Devon.

Ballet terms.Plié: French for 'bent', the plié is the knee-bending movement that begins nearly every ballet class.
Ballet terms.Pirouette: A whirl on one foot; the French word means 'spinning top'.
Ballet terms.Arabesque: A pose on one leg with the other extended behind; the name comes from the ornamental Arabic-style patterns.
Ballet terms.Jeté: French for 'thrown', it's a jump or leap from one foot to the other.
Ballet terms.Pas de deux: French for 'step of two', a duet in which a ballerina and a partner dance together.
Ballet terms.Tutu: The stiff, layered skirt; the long romantic version came in the 1830s, the short classical one later.
Ballet terms.Pointe: Dancers rise onto the tips of their toes in reinforced shoes, a trick first popularised in the 1830s.
Ballet terms.Barre: The rail along studio walls that dancers hold, which gives its name to barre fitness classes.
Ballet terms.Relevé: French for 'raised', a rise onto the balls of the feet or toes.
Ballet terms.Entrechat: A jump in which the legs beat together in the air; Nijinsky was famous for beating many times.
Ballet terms.Fouetté: A whipping turn on one leg; the Black Swan in Swan Lake famously performs 32 of them in a row.
Ballet terms.Moonwalk: Michael Jackson's backward glide, debuted on TV in 1983, wasn't his invention; street dancers had done versions of it for years.
Ballet terms.Dab: A pose popularised by Atlanta hip-hop and later by athletes and politicians, with the head tucked into the elbow; no ballet in sight.
Ballet terms.Windmill: A breakdance power move where the legs sweep in circles while the body spins on the back or shoulders.
Ballet terms.Shuffle: A ground-skimming step in many dance styles, from Melbourne rave dance to Chicago footwork, but not part of ballet vocabulary.
Ballet terms.Do-si-do: From the French dos-a-dos, 'back to back', this square-dance move has partners circle each other without touching hands.
Ballet terms.Cartwheel: A sideways handspring with straight arms and legs sweeping like a wheel's spokes; a gymnastics move, not ballet.
Ballet terms.Somersault: A full flip or roll of the body, head over heels, belonging to gymnastics rather than the ballet studio.
Ballet terms.Slam dunk: Basketball's high-flying finish, popularised by Wilt Chamberlain and Julius Erving, is leaps like ballet's but wearing sneakers.
Ballet terms.Touchdown: American football's scoring play is worth six points, and it earned its name from the early days when the ball had to be touched down.
Ballet terms.Haka: A Maori war dance with stamping and chanting, most famous worldwide when New Zealand's All Blacks perform it before rugby matches.
Ballet terms.Headspin: A breakdance move spun on the crown of the head, which dancers sometimes pad with a hat or cap.
Ballet terms.Robot: A 1980s street dance mimicking a machine, with stiff, jerky movements that came from funk and hip-hop in California.
Ballet terms.Worm: A breakdance floor move in which the body ripples like a worm, rolling a wave from head to toe.

Things that pop.Balloon: A latex balloon ruptures in a fraction of a millisecond, and the sudden snap of the rubber is the bang you hear.
Things that pop.Popcorn: A kernel pops when its trapped water turns to steam at about 180 C, bursting the starchy shell.
Things that pop.Bubble wrap: Invented in 1957 as textured wallpaper, bubble wrap only found fame as packaging a few years later.
Things that pop.Champagne cork: A cork can leave the bottle at roughly 50 km/h, and the cloud that forms is gas cooling as it expands.
Things that pop.Bubblegum: Walter Diemer's 1928 recipe was pink only because that was the dye he had on hand.
Things that pop.Toaster: Charles Strite patented the pop-up toaster in 1919 to stop restaurant bread from burning.
Things that pop.Firecracker: Invented in China roughly two thousand years ago, when bamboo was thrown on fires and exploded with a bang.
Things that pop.Jack-in-the-box: A coiled spring and a clown, its tune is typically Pop Goes the Weasel.
Things that pop.Knuckles: The pop is a bubble forming in the fluid between joints, not bones grinding, as scientists confirmed with MRI.
Things that pop.Weasel: Pop Goes the Weasel is an old English rhyme, and 'weasel' may mean something pawned.
Things that pop.Pillow: Pillows muffle noise and cushion your head, and old feather ones pop at the seams, but they're soft and silent.
Things that pop.Feather: A feather's barbs interlock like tiny hooks, so it keeps its shape and rarely makes noise.
Things that pop.Snowflake: Each snowflake grows around a speck of dust and falls silently, with six-fold symmetry from water's molecular shape.
Things that pop.Banana: Bananas are slightly radioactive from potassium-40, but harmless, and it never makes a pop.
Things that pop.Teddy bear: Named after Theodore Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a captive bear on a 1902 hunting trip; the cartoon and a toy maker followed.
Things that pop.Sock: Socks can crackle with static, but they never pop; a sock that vanishes in the wash is almost always trapped in the machine.
Things that pop.Rug: Rugs muffle sound; woven carpets date back thousands of years.
Things that pop.Cloud: Clouds hold huge weights of water, yet float silently.
Things that pop.Spaghetti: Raw spaghetti almost never snaps into two, a puzzle that stumped physicist Richard Feynman.
Things that pop.Cotton ball: Cotton balls are soft and silent, made from the fluffy fibres of a plant.
Things that pop.Bread: Bread bakes with yeast gas bubbles trapped in dough, but only a toaster pops it.
Things that pop.Cushion: Cushions compress silently, which is why they muffle noise.
Things that pop.Blanket: A blanket traps warmth by holding still air in its fibres, so it muffles rather than pops.
Things that pop.Slipper: Slippers are soft shoes and make little noise.

Things that can go flat.Tire: A tyre can lose pressure slowly even when undamaged, since rubber lets air seep through, so cars may drop a pound or so each month.
Things that can go flat.Soda: It goes flat as dissolved carbon dioxide escapes, and a warm bottle loses its fizz faster than a cold one.
Things that can go flat.Battery: A dead battery can often be revived briefly, and a car's can go flat if you leave the lights on overnight.
Things that can go flat.Singer: Singing flat means landing slightly below the correct pitch, and it often happens when a singer is tired.
Things that can go flat.Balloon: Helium escapes through the latex's tiny pores, so a helium balloon deflates in hours while an air-filled one lasts days.
Things that can go flat.Soufflé: The name comes from French for "puffed up", and a soufflé famously collapses when it cools or the oven door is opened.
Things that can go flat.Football: An American football can lose air over time, as seen in the 2015 Deflategate saga about the Patriots' footballs.
Things that can go flat.Lemonade: Fizzy lemonade goes flat once the gas escapes, and it is a good reason to screw the cap back on quickly.
Things that can go flat.Air mattress: It slowly sags overnight as air leaks out at the valve and seams, and cooling air in the room can contract as well.
Things that can go flat.Sparkling water: Fizz is carbonic acid breaking down into carbon dioxide gas, and a bottle fully opened can go flat within hours.
Things that can go flat.Mountain: Not flat by definition: a mountain is a high landform, and even the flattest peaks are called plateaus or mesas.
Things that can go flat.Pyramid: Its sides slope up to a point, and the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Things that can go flat.Cactus: Its spines are modified leaves, and a saguaro can grow arms only after about 70 years.
Things that can go flat.Candle: A candle burns down, but its wax does not go flat, and the flame draws wax up the wick as vapor.
Things that can go flat.Rainbow: It's a full circle of light, but from the ground you see just an arc, and you can only see a full circle from a plane.
Things that can go flat.Giraffe: It has seven neck bones, the same as people, but each is enormously long.
Things that can go flat.Book: A book can lie flat, but it doesn't go flat. Lay-flat binding is a feature designed for cookbooks and music scores.
Things that can go flat.Spoon: It has a bowl, and the oldest known spoons date back thousands of years.
Things that can go flat.Window: A window pane is already flat, so it can't "go" flat. The old myth of glass flowing downhill is false, as old panes are just uneven.
Things that can go flat.Statue: It stands proud in three dimensions, and the Statue of Liberty is made of copper that turned green with age.
Things that can go flat.Tree: Trees can grow for centuries; a bristlecone pine in California is more than 4,800 years old.
Things that can go flat.Ladder: Its rungs let you climb, and it can't go flat in the sense of losing air, though folding ones lie flat.
Things that can go flat.Igloo: Snow blocks trap air, so an igloo's inside can be warm, around freezing, even when it's far colder outside.
Things that can go flat.Teapot: A teapot's spout and lid work together to let tea pour smoothly, but it does not go flat.

Sports with weight classes.Boxing: Fighters are split into divisions from strawweight to heavyweight, and weigh in the day before so they can rehydrate before the bout.
Sports with weight classes.Wrestling: Classes keep fighters evenly matched by size, and wrestlers often cut water weight before weigh-ins, which is a risky habit.
Sports with weight classes.Judo: Divided into seven weight classes at the Olympics, the sport was created in 1882 by Kano Jigoro, and its name means gentle way.
Sports with weight classes.Weightlifting: Lifters compete in bodyweight classes, with barbells of 20 kg for men and 15 kg for women, so size can't decide the winner alone.
Sports with weight classes.Taekwondo: Korean martial art with Olympic weight divisions, and it is famed for high kicks, with electronic body sensors scoring hits.
Sports with weight classes.MMA: Mixed martial arts has divisions from flyweight to heavyweight, and the sport's modern form began with the UFC in 1993.
Sports with weight classes.Rowing: Lightweight rowing has weight limits, and it's the only Olympic rowing group with a cap, since heavier rowers tend to have more power.
Sports with weight classes.Kickboxing: A striking sport with weight classes, mixing boxing punches and kicks, and it developed in 1960s Japan and the US.
Sports with weight classes.Powerlifting: Lifters are placed in classes by body weight, and compete in squat, bench press and deadlift, three lifts totalled for the score.
Sports with weight classes.Sumo: No weight classes in Japan's top ranks, so a 100 kg wrestler can face one twice that size, and that is a major part of its drama.
Sports with weight classes.Fencing: Athletes duel by weapon, foil, epee or sabre, not by weight, and the sport uses wired suits to register touches.
Sports with weight classes.Tennis: There are no weight classes, so slender and heavy players meet on the same court, with skill, speed and serve power evening things out.
Sports with weight classes.Swimming: No weight classes, and long arms and big feet help, which is why you see tall swimmers, but none are separated by weight.
Sports with weight classes.Gymnastics: No weight classes, but gymnasts are small because of the strength-to-weight ratio, which helps with spins.
Sports with weight classes.Archery: Competitors are grouped by bow type and not body weight, and anyone can compete.
Sports with weight classes.Golf: No weight classes, and players from small to large compete together, with handicaps being the equalizer.
Sports with weight classes.Basketball: Height matters far more than weight, and no classes divide players.
Sports with weight classes.Cycling: No weight classes, though lightweight climbers excel in the mountains, and the bike has minimum weight limits.
Sports with weight classes.Sprinting: No weight classes in athletics, and the same 100 m race includes lighter and heavier runners.
Sports with weight classes.Shooting: Shooters compete in categories by gun type and not by body weight.
Sports with weight classes.Curling: No weight classes, but the stones do weigh around 20 kg, and that is the only weight that counts.
Sports with weight classes.Diving: No weight classes, and divers are judged on form, with small splashes scoring higher.
Sports with weight classes.Equestrian: Riders are not divided by weight, though in racing the jockeys carry assigned weights, which is a similar principle.
Sports with weight classes.Table tennis: No weight classes, and a ball weighs just 2.7 grams, which is the only weight rule.

Things that have a cap.Pen: Pen caps often have a tiny hole so that a swallowed cap won't fully block a child's airway, a safety rule in many countries.
Things that have a cap.Marker: Permanent markers dry out fast when uncapped because their solvent evaporates, so the cap seals in a damp tip.
Things that have a cap.Water bottle: Screw caps on bottles are a modern convenience; the crown cap for glass bottles, patented in 1892, has 21 teeth.
Things that have a cap.Toothpaste: A flip-top cap lets a tube stand on its head, a trick that helps squeeze out the last bit of paste.
Things that have a cap.Camera lens: A lens cap protects the glass from scratches and dust, and forgetting to take it off is a classic photographer's blunder.
Things that have a cap.Glue stick: The cap keeps the glue from drying out, and a glue stick can be left capless for just a few hours before it hardens.
Things that have a cap.Highlighter: The cap is crucial because the fluorescent ink dries out quickly, and a cap left off can ruin a highlighter overnight.
Things that have a cap.Lipstick: The lipstick tube was invented in 1915 by Maurice Levy, and its cap is a snug sleeve that keeps the stick from smudging.
Things that have a cap.Fire hydrant: The caps on a hydrant cover its outlets, and firefighters remove them with a special wrench to hook up a hose.
Things that have a cap.Mushroom: A mushroom's cap holds the gills or pores that release spores, and some caps can spread thousands of spores per second.
Things that have a cap.Lip balm: Lip balm caps are tiny, and its balm is often made from beeswax, which is why it protects against wind.
Things that have a cap.Nail polish: The cap carries the brush, and the thin neck of the bottle wipes off extra polish as you pull it out.
Things that have a cap.Pencil: Pencil leads are really graphite and clay, and a pencil has no cap, though an eraser end often sits at the other end.
Things that have a cap.Crayon: No cap needed; crayons are solid wax and pigment, and they won't dry out, though they do melt in a hot car.
Things that have a cap.Eraser: Erasers lack a cap, though some come with a paper sleeve; the pink rubber is often synthetic these days.
Things that have a cap.Ruler: A ruler has no cap, just marks along an edge, and rulers date back to the Indus Valley civilization over 4,000 years ago.
Things that have a cap.Stapler: It has no cap, but it does have a hinged lid for loading a strip of staples, so that is a near miss.
Things that have a cap.Scissors: Scissors usually have no cap, though safety scissors for children often come with a plastic guard over the blades.
Things that have a cap.Paper clip: A paper clip is a bent wire with no cap, and it was widely sold by the 1890s, though who invented it is unclear.
Things that have a cap.Mug: A mug has no cap, though a travel mug does come with a lid, which is a different thing.
Things that have a cap.Book: A book has a cover but no cap, and the jacket sleeve is there to protect the hardback underneath.
Things that have a cap.Spoon: A spoon has no cap, and the spoon is an open, uncovered tool for eating.
Things that have a cap.Plate: A plate has no cap, and it is an open, flat dish that is meant to be filled and not sealed.
Things that have a cap.Candle: A candle has no cap, but a snuffer cap can be used to put out the flame without smoke.

Makeup products.Mascara: Mascara dates back to ancient Egypt, where kohl and soot darkened lashes, and the modern tube arrived in the 1910s.
Makeup products.Eyeliner: Ancient Egyptians lined their eyes with kohl, partly for style and partly to cut the sun's glare.
Makeup products.Lipstick: Lipstick has been around for about 5,000 years, and red shades were once made from crushed insects called cochineal.
Makeup products.Blush: Blush adds color to the cheeks, and its history runs from ancient plant dyes to the compact powder of today.
Makeup products.Foundation: Foundation evens out skin tone, and modern shade ranges can run to dozens of tones to fit different complexions.
Makeup products.Concealer: Concealer is usually a shade lighter than foundation, since its job is to brighten shadows like under-eye circles.
Makeup products.Eyeshadow: Many eyeshadows get their shimmer from mica, a glittering mineral, and the sparkle comes from tiny reflective flakes.
Makeup products.Bronzer: Bronzer gives a sun-kissed glow without a tan, and it is a modern relic of Coco Chanel making tans fashionable in the 1920s.
Makeup products.Lip gloss: Lip gloss reflects light because of oils and waxes, and early versions were simply petroleum jelly rubbed on the lips.
Makeup products.Face powder: Face powder sets makeup and absorbs shine, and historically it was ground rice or even toxic white lead.
Makeup products.Lip liner: Lip liner outlines the mouth and stops lipstick from feathering into fine lines around it.
Makeup products.Shampoo: Shampoo is a hair product, not makeup, and the word comes from a Hindi word for head massage, champo.
Makeup products.Toothpaste: Toothpaste is hygiene, not makeup, and its fluoride has been credited with big falls in cavities since the 1950s.
Makeup products.Deodorant: Deodorant hides odor, while antiperspirant blocks sweat, and it is care rather than color.
Makeup products.Razor: A razor is grooming, not makeup, and the first safety razor with a disposable blade came around 1901.
Makeup products.Shaving cream: Shaving cream softens whiskers and helps the blade glide, which is care rather than cosmetics.
Makeup products.Mouthwash: Mouthwash rinses the mouth and is hygiene, and it is meant to be spat out, never swallowed.
Makeup products.Conditioner: Conditioner smooths hair rather than painting the face, so it is personal care, not makeup.
Makeup products.Body wash: Body wash cleans the skin and is a bathroom product, not something you wear to look different.
Makeup products.Dental floss: Dental floss is hygiene, not makeup, and was first made from silk thread by a dentist in the early 1800s.
Makeup products.Hair gel: Hair gel is for styling hair, which is a different category from cosmetics worn on the face.
Makeup products.Cologne: Cologne is fragrance, not makeup, and the name comes from Cologne, Germany, where Eau de Cologne was created in 1709.
Makeup products.Bath bomb: A bath bomb fizzes because citric acid and baking soda react in water, and it is bath time, not makeup.
Makeup products.Nail clippers: Nail clippers are grooming tools, a different group from color products like polish.

Organs of the human body.Heart: The heart beats about 100,000 times a day and pumps roughly 7,000 liters of blood.
Organs of the human body.Liver: The liver is the only internal organ that can regrow, and it can regenerate from a surprisingly small piece.
Organs of the human body.Lung: Your right lung is slightly larger than the left, which makes room for the heart on the left.
Organs of the human body.Kidney: Kidneys filter all your blood about 40 times a day, and you can live a healthy life with just one.
Organs of the human body.Spleen: The spleen filters old blood cells and helps fight infection, but you can live without it.
Organs of the human body.Pancreas: The pancreas does two jobs at once: it makes digestive enzymes and the hormone insulin.
Organs of the human body.Stomach: The stomach's acid is strong enough to dissolve metal, so a mucus lining replaces its surface every few days.
Organs of the human body.Gallbladder: The gallbladder stores bile, and many people have it removed with little change to their lives.
Organs of the human body.Brain: The brain uses about 20 percent of the body's energy while being only 2 percent of its weight.
Organs of the human body.Bladder: A bladder can stretch to hold about half a liter or more before the urge to go becomes strong.
Organs of the human body.Skin: Skin is the largest organ, covering about two square meters and renewing itself roughly every month.
Organs of the human body.Thyroid: The thyroid is shaped like a butterfly and controls your metabolism. It sits in the front of the neck.
Organs of the human body.Femur: The femur is a bone, and the longest in the body, and it's not an organ in the usual sense.
Organs of the human body.Biceps: Biceps is a muscle, one of many in the body. Muscles are tissues, not usually called organs.
Organs of the human body.Tendon: A tendon joins muscle to bone, so it's a tissue, not an organ.
Organs of the human body.Patella: The patella, or kneecap, is a bone. It protects the knee joint.
Organs of the human body.Cartilage: Cartilage is a tough, flexible tissue found in joints, ears and the nose. It's a tissue, not an organ.
Organs of the human body.Plasma: Plasma is the pale yellow fluid in blood, making up about 55 percent of it. It's a fluid, not an organ.
Organs of the human body.Hemoglobin: Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, and it's what makes blood red.
Organs of the human body.Collagen: Collagen is the most abundant protein in your body, and it gives skin and tendons their strength.
Organs of the human body.Vertebra: A vertebra is a bone of the spine, and it's not an organ.
Organs of the human body.Ligament: Ligaments connect bone to bone. They are tissue, and no one calls them organs.
Organs of the human body.Platelet: Platelets are tiny cell fragments that clot blood. They're cells, not organs.
Organs of the human body.Eyelash: Eyelashes are hairs, so they're a trap here. Skin is an organ, but a lash is only a tiny part of it.

Things that go pop.Balloon: A balloon pops because the stretched rubber tears faster than the air can escape, and the crack is a small shockwave.
Things that go pop.Popcorn: Each kernel pops when its trapped water turns to steam at around 180 degrees Celsius, turning the starch inside out.
Things that go pop.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap was invented in 1957 as textured wallpaper, and only later found its fame as packaging.
Things that go pop.Champagne cork: A champagne cork can leave the bottle at around 50 kilometers per hour, so opening it carefully is not just for show.
Things that go pop.Cracking knuckles: The pop of a knuckle is a gas bubble forming in the joint fluid, and studies have not linked it to arthritis.
Things that go pop.Bubble gum: Bubble gum pops because the stretched film of gum thins until it bursts; the first successful version was pink only because pink dye was on hand.
Things that go pop.Popping candy: Popping candy is hard sugar with pressurized carbon dioxide trapped inside; the gas escapes with a crackle as it melts on your tongue.
Things that go pop.Toaster: A toaster pops by design: a spring-loaded carriage pushes the bread up the moment a timer or sensor stops the heat.
Things that go pop.Cork gun: A cork gun fires by compressed air or spring, and the 'pop' is the sound of the cork leaving the barrel.
Things that go pop.Feather: A feather falls so slowly because it is light and has a lot of drag, which is why it can drift without making any noise.
Things that go pop.Pillow: A pillow muffles any sound, but if you press down on a sealed, air-filled one hard enough, it can burst with a pop.
Things that go pop.Snowflake: A snowflake lands silently, and each one is a cluster of ice crystals shaped by the temperature and humidity it fell through.
Things that go pop.Cotton ball: A cotton ball is soft fiber that soaks up impacts, so it can hit the floor without any sound at all.
Things that go pop.Butterfly: A butterfly's wings are covered in tiny overlapping scales, and the beat of its wings is almost silent.
Things that go pop.Silk scarf: Silk is a fiber produced by silkworms, and a single cocoon is one thread that can be about a kilometer long.
Things that go pop.Whisper: A whisper has no vibrating vocal cords, so it contains only airflow noise; it is a hiss, not a pop.
Things that go pop.Sponge: Sponges are animals as well as bath items; the natural kind has no organs, and its pores hush any sound that touches it.
