Things that go pop.Tissue: A tissue is built from short wood fibers that soak up moisture; nothing about it can pop, just crumple.
Things that go pop.Cloud: A typical fluffy cloud holds hundreds of tonnes of water, yet floats because that water is spread as tiny droplets in rising air.
Things that go pop.Leaf: A fresh leaf can crack when folded, but a falling one just rustles and glides, spinning to slow its descent.
Things that go pop.Marshmallow: Marshmallows were originally made from the sap of the marsh mallow plant; today's version squishes, it does not pop.
Things that go pop.Moth: Some moths are so quiet that bats cannot hear them, and others even jam bat sonar with clicks of their own.
Things that go pop.Sock: A sock is soft knit fabric, so it falls or lands without a sound, and a stretched sock only pops when it tears.
Things that go pop.Velvet: Velvet's soft pile is made by weaving two layers of fabric at once and then slicing them apart, and it absorbs sound.

Weird animals that actually exist.Axolotl: An axolotl is a Mexican salamander that stays a larval-looking form all its life, and it can regrow limbs and even parts of its heart.
Weird animals that actually exist.Aye-aye: The aye-aye is a Madagascar lemur that taps trees with a long thin middle finger to find grubs, and it has been feared in local folklore.
Weird animals that actually exist.Blobfish: The blobfish looks like a sad blob only when hauled up; underwater, the deep-sea fish looks much more like a normal fish.
Weird animals that actually exist.Narwhal: The narwhal's 'horn' is a spiral tooth that can reach about three meters, and it has sensors that detect the water's saltiness.
Weird animals that actually exist.Quokka: The quokka, a small Australian marsupial, is known as the happiest animal because its mouth looks like it is smiling.
Weird animals that actually exist.Pangolin: Pangolins are scaly mammals that roll into a ball, and they are the most trafficked mammal in the world.
Weird animals that actually exist.Dik-dik: A dik-dik is a tiny African antelope the size of a hare, and the name comes from the sound of the female's alarm call.
Weird animals that actually exist.Wombat: A wombat produces cube-shaped droppings, the only animal known to do so, and it uses them to mark territory.
Weird animals that actually exist.Okapi: The okapi looks like a zebra-striped horse but is a close relative of the giraffe, and it was only found by scientists in 1901.
Weird animals that actually exist.Platypus: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs, has a duck bill, and the male has venomous spurs on its hind legs.
Weird animals that actually exist.Capybara: The capybara is the largest rodent, up to about 60 kilograms, and it is so calm that other animals will sit on it.
Weird animals that actually exist.Numbat: The numbat is a small Australian marsupial that eats thousands of termites a day and has stripes on its back.
Weird animals that actually exist.Tapir: A tapir has a flexible short trunk and is a distant relative of horses and rhinos, and its calves are born with spots and stripes.
Weird animals that actually exist.Jackalope: The jackalope, a rabbit with antlers, is American folklore, and was probably inspired by rabbits with a viral growth disease.
Weird animals that actually exist.Griffin: The griffin has the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, and it appears in art from ancient Persia and Greece.
Weird animals that actually exist.Unicorn: The unicorn may come from ancient reports of the Indian rhinoceros, and it is the national animal of Scotland.
Weird animals that actually exist.Hippogriff: The hippogriff, half horse and half eagle, was invented by the Italian poet Ariosto in the 1500s.
Weird animals that actually exist.Chupacabra: The chupacabra is a monster said to drain goats, with reports starting in Puerto Rico in 1995 and no real evidence.
Weird animals that actually exist.Pegasus: Pegasus is the winged horse of Greek myth, born from Medusa's blood, and he also lends his name to a constellation.
Weird animals that actually exist.Bigfoot: Bigfoot is a legendary ape-like creature of North America, and no solid evidence has ever been found.
Weird animals that actually exist.Yeti: The yeti is a mythical ape-like creature of the Himalayas, and DNA tests of supposed relics have pointed to bears.
Weird animals that actually exist.Kraken: The kraken was a giant sea monster of Scandinavian legend, probably inspired by the giant squid, which is real.
Weird animals that actually exist.Manticore: The manticore is a mythic beast with a human face, a lion body, and a scorpion tail, first described by a Greek writer in Persia.
Weird animals that actually exist.Phoenix: The phoenix is a legendary bird that burns and is reborn from its ashes, and Phoenix, Arizona, is named after it.

Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Résumé: Hiring managers often spend only seconds on a first scan of a résumé, so a clear one-page layout helps.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Portfolio: Designers, writers and photographers lean on a portfolio because it shows your work instead of just describing it.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Pen: A pen shows you're ready, and unlike a phone it keeps your attention on the interviewer while you jot something down.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Notepad: Taking brief notes shows you're listening, and it gives you a place to jot answers and follow-up thoughts.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Photo ID: Many offices require photo ID at the security desk before you can go in, so bring a passport or driver's licence.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Reference list: A prepared list of references with contact details saves time, but always ask those people for permission first.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Business cards: Business cards trace back to the visiting cards used in 17th-century Europe, and handing one over still shows professionalism.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Questions to ask: Interviewers nearly always ask whether you have questions, and asking good ones shows genuine interest in the role.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Cover letter: A cover letter lets you explain why you fit the role, covering things a résumé's bullet points can't capture.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Pet snake: A pet snake might make the interviewer scream, and it would be hard to concentrate on your résumé.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Sleeping bag: A sleeping bag is for camping; showing up with one suggests you plan to nap instead of impress.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Karaoke mic: A karaoke mic belongs at a party, whereas an interviewer wants a conversation, not a performance.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Pyjamas: Pyjamas are for bedtime, and even remote interviews call for smart clothes, ideally one level above what the job requires.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Beach towel: A beach towel signals you're headed to the shore afterwards, which isn't the first impression to give.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Air horn: An air horn can reach about 120 decibels, loud enough to damage hearing and empty an office.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Water gun: A water gun might win a laugh, but it would likely end the interview as soon as someone gets squirted.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Party popper: A party popper celebrates a job after you win it, not before; confetti during the interview is unwise.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Inflatable flamingo: A pool-toy flamingo may charm at a party, but in an office it signals you didn't take the interview seriously.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Bag of crisps: Crunching snacks in an interview is distracting, and greasy fingers don't help a first handshake.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Leaf blower: Leaf blowers can exceed 90 decibels, far too loud for a quiet office conversation, and awkward to carry in.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Whoopee cushion: A whoopee cushion is a classic prank; humour is welcome in moderation, but this will end the interview.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Bongo drums: Bongo drums are small Cuban hand drums, and they're hard to carry past reception and harder to explain.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Bubble machine: A bubble machine floods a room with soap bubbles, great for parties and awful for polished interview carpets.
Sensible things to bring to a job interv.Fishing rod: A fishing rod is for the lake; unless you're interviewing to be a fishing guide, leave it in the car.

Transformers Autobots.Optimus Prime: Peter Cullen voiced the Autobot leader, and he drew on his brother's tough-but-gentle nature as inspiration for the role.
Transformers Autobots.Bumblebee: In the original cartoon he was a yellow VW Beetle, but in the recent films he is a Camaro, and he cannot speak in them.
Transformers Autobots.Jazz: This Autobot first transformed into a Porsche 935, and his cool talk made him a fan favorite in the 1980s cartoon.
Transformers Autobots.Ironhide: The Autobot weapons specialist was a red van in the original toy line, and the character has appeared across eras.
Transformers Autobots.Ratchet: The medic of the Autobots, who first appeared as an ambulance, was named after a tool, since ratchet is a wrench.
Transformers Autobots.Wheeljack: This inventor Autobot is known for explosions in the lab, and his original toy was a Lancia Stratos Turbo.
Transformers Autobots.Grimlock: The leader of the Dinobots turns into a Tyrannosaurus, and the 1980s cartoon made him famously talk in a clumsy way.
Transformers Autobots.Hot Rod: He became Rodimus Prime in the 1986 movie, which is the one that famously killed off Optimus Prime.
Transformers Autobots.Arcee: She was the first female Autobot, introduced in the 1986 movie, as the line had been all male before then.
Transformers Autobots.Ultra Magnus: This tall Autobot was a carrier who transformed into a car transporter, and in the 1986 movie he leads in Prime's absence.
Transformers Autobots.Megatron: This is the Decepticon leader and Optimus Prime's rival, who became a gun in the 1980s toys, so he is not an Autobot.
Transformers Autobots.Starscream: The jet-based Decepticon is always plotting to overthrow Megatron, so he has never been on the Autobot side.
Transformers Autobots.Soundwave: This Decepticon communications officer turns into a cassette player and sends out tape minions, and he is a Decepticon.
Transformers Autobots.Shockwave: The one-eyed Decepticon scientist is a cold logician, and he first transformed into a laser gun.
Transformers Autobots.Devastator: Six Constructicon Decepticons combine to form this giant construction robot, so he works for Megatron.
Transformers Autobots.Galvatron: He is Megatron rebuilt by Unicron in the 1986 movie, which makes him a Decepticon.
Transformers Autobots.Blitzwing: This Decepticon has three forms, including a jet and a tank, and he is known for a split personality.
Transformers Autobots.Thundercracker: This Decepticon jet is one of Starscream's fellow seekers, and he is known for his gloomy attitude.
Transformers Autobots.Skywarp: The Decepticon jet can teleport, and he is part of the Seeker trio, so he is no Autobot.
Transformers Autobots.Ravage: This Decepticon cat is one of Soundwave's cassettes, and he is a panther-like spy.
Transformers Autobots.Unicron: This planet-eating chaos god is bigger than the Autobots and Decepticons, and he is a villain from the 1986 film.
Transformers Autobots.Barricade: This Decepticon turns into a police car in the 2007 movie, and the name suits his Decepticon-police look.
Transformers Autobots.Laserbeak: This condor cassette is one of Soundwave's minions, which makes him a Decepticon.
Transformers Autobots.Bonecrusher: This Decepticon's bulldozer form appeared in the 2007 film, and he is a brutish demolition expert.

Ballets.Swan Lake: Tchaikovsky's 1877 ballet flopped at its premiere, and it was only after his death, in a 1895 revival, that it became beloved; the dual role Odette/Odile is a ballerina's ultimate test.
Ballets.The Nutcracker: Tchaikovsky's 1892 ballet was only a modest success at first, and now earns many US companies a large share of their yearly income.
Ballets.Giselle: Premiered in Paris in 1841, this ballet about a peasant girl who dies of heartbreak features the Wilis, ghosts of jilted brides.
Ballets.Coppélia: Delibes's comic 1870 ballet follows a young man smitten with a life-sized doll, and is one of the great romantic comedies of dance.
Ballets.The Firebird: Stravinsky's 1910 score, his first for the Ballets Russes, made him famous overnight, and it is based on a Russian folk tale.
Ballets.La Bayadère: Marius Petipa's 1877 ballet set in India is known for the Kingdom of the Shades scene, where dozens of dancers descend a ramp in an unbroken line.
Ballets.The Sleeping Beauty: Tchaikovsky's 1890 ballet, based on the fairy tale, was his own favourite among his ballets.
Ballets.The Rite of Spring: Stravinsky's pagan-ritual ballet reportedly provoked shouting and near-rioting at its 1913 Paris premiere, though accounts are exaggerated.
Ballets.Petrushka: Stravinsky's 1911 ballet tells of a puppet who comes to life and falls in love, and it is known for its bold use of two keys at once.
Ballets.La Sylphide: This 1832 ballet is among the first Romantic ballets, and it made pointe work and ethereal winged spirits fashionable.
Ballets.La Traviata: Verdi's 1853 opera is sung, not danced, so no ballet here.
Ballets.Aida: Verdi's Egyptian opera features a ballet inside it, but the work itself is an opera.
Ballets.Tosca: Puccini's thriller is an opera; its stage direction involves a murder and a leap, not a pas de deux.
Ballets.La Bohème: Puccini's story of poor Parisian artists is an opera, not a ballet.
Ballets.The Magic Flute: Mozart's fairy-tale piece is an opera with spoken dialogue.
Ballets.Rigoletto: Verdi's court-jester tragedy is an opera, centred on singers rather than dancers.
Ballets.Turandot: Puccini's last opera, left unfinished at his death, is sung throughout; its tenor aria Nessun dorma isn't danced either.
Ballets.Don Giovanni: Mozart's opera about the seducer is sung from start to finish, not danced.
Ballets.Cats: Lloyd Webber's musical is heavily choreographed, but it is a musical, not a classical ballet.
Ballets.Hamilton: Lin-Manuel Miranda's hip-hop musical is a musical, though it won many awards for choreography.
Ballets.The Four Seasons: Vivaldi's concertos are music alone, though ballets have been set to them.
Ballets.Für Elise: Beethoven's famous piano piece is a short solo work, though it's about as recognisable as any ballet tune.
Ballets.Messiah: Handel's 1741 oratorio includes the Hallelujah chorus, and is not a staged ballet.
Ballets.Moonlight Sonata: Beethoven's piano sonata got its nickname after his death, and it was never intended as a ballet.

Sorted into Gryffindor.Harry Potter: Harry Potter was nearly placed in Slytherin, but the Sorting Hat honored his wish and chose Gryffindor.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Hermione Granger: Hermione Granger got her name from a Shakespeare character in The Winter's Tale, and Rowling picked it as an unusual name.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Ron Weasley: Ron Weasley is the sixth of seven Weasley children, and he plays a lifesize wizard chess game during the Philosopher's Stone.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Neville Longbottom: Neville Longbottom was almost placed in Hufflepuff, but he later destroys Voldemort's snake Nagini with the Sword of Gryffindor.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Ginny Weasley: Ginny Weasley is the only girl born into her generation of the large Weasley family, after six brothers.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Seamus Finnigan: Seamus Finnigan is a half-blood who keeps accidentally blowing things up, thanks to his wand-work.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Dean Thomas: Dean Thomas is a talented artist and Gryffindor dormitory-mate who was raised by a Muggle father.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Lavender Brown: Lavender Brown, a Gryffindor who dated Ron in sixth year, was later attacked by the werewolf Fenrir Greyback and survived.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Parvati Patil: Parvati Patil is a Gryffindor and a member of Dumbledore's Army; she went with Harry to the Yule Ball.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Oliver Wood: Oliver Wood, the Gryffindor Quidditch captain and Keeper, is obsessed with winning and later plays for Puddlemere United.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Lee Jordan: Lee Jordan is the Gryffindor student who provides lively commentary on Quidditch matches, to McGonagall's despair.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Colin Creevey: Colin Creevey is a young Gryffindor fan of Harry's who always carries a camera and, tragically, dies in the Battle of Hogwarts.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Draco Malfoy: Draco is a Slytherin, and his name echoes the Latin for dragon, while his father bought the team Nimbus 2001 brooms.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Vincent Crabbe: Crabbe is a Slytherin; Harry and Ron once disguised themselves as him and Goyle with Polyjuice Potion in Chamber of Secrets.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Gregory Goyle: Goyle is a Slytherin who, alongside Crabbe, was Draco's shadow, and neither was known for their brains.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Pansy Parkinson: Pansy is a Slytherin, a Draco devotee who, in the final battle, suggests handing Harry over to Voldemort.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Luna Lovegood: Luna is a Ravenclaw, a house that prizes wit, and she wears radish earrings and wonders about Nargles.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Cho Chang: Cho is a Ravenclaw and a Seeker for her house, and she shares Harry's first kiss in Order of the Phoenix.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Cedric Diggory: Cedric was a Hufflepuff, the house for loyal and fair-minded students, and he tied Harry for the Triwizard Cup.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Padma Patil: Padma is a Ravenclaw, not a Gryffindor, though her identical twin Parvati was sorted into Gryffindor.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Ernie Macmillan: Ernie is a Hufflepuff who once suspected Harry of being the Heir of Slytherin, and later apologized.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Hannah Abbott: Hannah is a Hufflepuff and a member of Dumbledore's Army; Rowling says she grew up to run the Leaky Cauldron.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Tom Riddle: Tom Riddle was a Slytherin before he became Voldemort, a name that's an anagram of his birth name.
Sorted into Gryffindor.Blaise Zabini: Blaise is a Slytherin, and Rowling gave his glamorous mother a reputation for having married seven times.

Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Dune: Frank Herbert's 1965 desert-planet epic, built around the spice melange, was inspired by his study of ecology.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Foundation: Isaac Asimov's saga of psychohistory won a special Hugo in 1966 as the best all-time series.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Neuromancer: William Gibson's 1984 debut is the first novel to win the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Solaris: Stanisław Lem's 1961 story of a sentient ocean planet; he disliked Tarkovsky's famous film version.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.The Time Machine: Wells's 1895 novel coined the time machine; it is a science fiction novel with no magic.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Fahrenheit 451: Bradbury said 451 degrees Fahrenheit is the temperature at which book paper burns.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Ender's Game: Orson Scott Card's 1985 novel grew from a short story published in 1977.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.The Martian: Andy Weir first posted this story chapter by chapter on his own website before it was published.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Hyperion: Dan Simmons's 1989 novel is structured like Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, with pilgrims telling stories.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Starship Troopers: Heinlein's 1959 novel is the source of a satirical 1997 film directed by Paul Verhoeven.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Ringworld: Larry Niven's 1970 novel imagines a ring-shaped world, which fans noted was unstable; the sequel added fixes.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.War of the Worlds: Wells's 1898 Martian invasion remains a pillar of science fiction.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.The Hobbit: Tolkien's 1937 prequel to The Lord of the Rings is fantasy with dragons and a wizard.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.A Game of Thrones: George R. R. Martin's 1996 epic begins A Song of Ice and Fire, a fantasy of kingdoms.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.The Name of the Wind: Patrick Rothfuss's 2007 novel follows a magical musician-wizard, so it's fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Mistborn: Brandon Sanderson's 2006 novel features metal-based magic called Allomancy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.The Colour of Magic: Terry Pratchett's 1983 comic fantasy launched his Discworld series.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Eragon: Christopher Paolini's 2002 dragon-rider tale is fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Stardust: Neil Gaiman's 1999 fairy tale of a falling star is fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Coraline: Gaiman's 2002 dark tale of a button-eyed Other Mother is fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.American Gods: Neil Gaiman's 2001 novel about old gods in modern America is fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.Good Omens: Terry Pratchett and Neil Gaiman's 1990 comedy about an angel and a demon is fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.The Silmarillion: Tolkien's mythology of Middle-earth, published in 1977, is high fantasy.
Science fiction (not fantasy) novels.A Wizard of Earthsea: Ursula K. Le Guin's 1968 wizard-school story is fantasy.

Shakespeare characters who die in their.Hamlet: Hamlet is killed by a poisoned sword in the last scene, moments after his mother and his uncle die too.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Ophelia: Ophelia drowns in a stream after losing her mind, and her death is reported by Gertrude rather than seen on stage.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Polonius: He is stabbed through a tapestry while spying on Hamlet and his mother.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Mercutio: His last words, 'A plague o' both your houses', damn both feuding families.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Tybalt: Tybalt is killed by Romeo in a street fight, in revenge for Mercutio, which leads to Romeo's banishment.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Lady Macbeth: She sleepwalks and rubs her hands, and dies off stage, apparently by suicide.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Duncan: King Duncan is murdered in his sleep by Macbeth while a guest in his castle, early in the play.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Banquo: Banquo is murdered by Macbeth's hired killers, and his ghost appears at the banquet.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Desdemona: Desdemona is smothered by her husband Othello, who wrongly believes she's been unfaithful.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Cordelia: Cordelia, Lear's loyal daughter, is hanged in prison on orders, moments before help arrives.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.King Lear: King Lear dies of grief, carrying the body of his youngest daughter Cordelia.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Julius Caesar: Julius Caesar dies in Act 3, scene 1, though the play is named for him, and Brutus has more lines.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Cleopatra: Cleopatra ends her life with a poisonous asp, rather than being paraded through Rome.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Horatio: Horatio survives, even wants to drink the poison and die too, but Hamlet makes him live to tell the story.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Fortinbras: Fortinbras, prince of Norway, arrives after the carnage and takes the Danish crown.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Macduff: Macduff kills Macbeth, fulfilling the prophecy, because he was 'untimely ripped' from his mother's womb.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Malcolm: Malcolm, Duncan's son, survives and is crowned king of Scotland at the end of Macbeth.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Fleance: Fleance, Banquo's son, escapes the murderers who kill his father, and the witches say his line will be kings.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Iago: Iago, Othello's villain, is arrested and refuses to explain; he survives the play, at least onstage.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Cassio: Cassio is wounded by Iago's agents in Othello, but he survives and is left in charge of Cyprus.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Edgar: Edgar survives King Lear and is left to rebuild the kingdom after the bloodbath.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Friar Laurence: Friar Laurence survives Romeo and Juliet and explains the tragic story to the Prince.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Benvolio: Benvolio is Romeo's cousin and friend, who survives to give the Prince his account of the brawl.
Shakespeare characters who die in their.Prospero: Prospero survives The Tempest, gives up magic, and sails home to Milan.

Airlines.Lufthansa: Germany's flag carrier, whose name means roughly 'air Hansa'. It's a founding member of Star Alliance, the first global airline alliance, formed in 1997.
Airlines.Ryanair: Ireland's budget giant often carries more passengers per year than any other European airline, and built its empire on cheap fares plus fees for nearly everything extra.
Airlines.Emirates: Based in Dubai, it flies a fleet made up almost entirely of wide-body jets, including one of the world's largest collections of Airbus A380 superjumbos.
Airlines.Qantas: Its name began as an acronym for Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services, and it is one of the oldest airlines in the world, founded in 1920.
Airlines.Delta: Delta started in 1925 as a crop-dusting company in Georgia, spraying cotton fields against boll weevils, long before it carried passengers.
Airlines.KLM: Founded in 1919, KLM is the oldest airline still operating under its original name, and the Dutch royal title 'Koninklijke' was granted in its first year.
Airlines.easyJet: The orange-liveried British carrier was founded in 1995 by Stelios Haji-Ioannou, who famously launched it with just two leased planes.
Airlines.Air France: France's national carrier merged with KLM in 2004, forming a group that still runs both brands separately from hubs in Paris and Amsterdam.
Airlines.Cathay Pacific: Hong Kong's flag carrier was founded in 1946 by an American and an Australian pilot who flew surplus WWII Douglas DC-3s, one nicknamed Betsy.
Airlines.Southwest: This US carrier built its model on one aircraft type, the Boeing 737, which kept maintenance and crew training simple and fares low.
Airlines.Aeroflot: Once the Soviet Union's only airline and among the largest in the world, it still carries Russia's flag, and its logo keeps the winged hammer-and-sickle look.
Airlines.Etihad: Founded in 2003, the Abu Dhabi flag carrier takes its name from the Arabic word for 'union', echoing the United Arab Emirates.
Airlines.Singapore Airlines: Famous for the 'Singapore Girl' ad icon, it regularly tops best-airline rankings and has operated some of the longest nonstop flights in the world.
Airlines.Boeing: Boeing is an aircraft maker, not an airline. It began in 1916 in a Seattle boathouse, and its 747 jumbo jet was the world's largest passenger plane for decades.
Airlines.Airbus: Airbus builds planes rather than flying them. It's a European consortium born in 1970, and its A380 is the largest passenger airliner ever built.
Airlines.Heathrow: An airport, not an airline. London's biggest hub is among the busiest in the world and sits on land that was once a small farming hamlet.
Airlines.Changi: Singapore's airport is a famous trap: it's not an airline. It's often voted world's best and has a butterfly garden and a huge indoor waterfall.
Airlines.Schiphol: Amsterdam's airport, not an airline. Its name means 'ship hole' because it sits on a drained lake bed once known for shipwrecks, and sits below sea level.
Airlines.O'Hare: Chicago's big airport, not a carrier. Its name honors Butch O'Hare, a WWII navy pilot and Medal of Honor recipient, and its code ORD comes from Orchard Field.
Airlines.Gatwick: London's second airport, not an airline. Its single runway handles more flights than any other single-runway airport in the world.
Airlines.Expedia: A travel booking website, not an airline. It started in 1996 as a Microsoft division and sells flights from the very carriers listed here.
Airlines.Hertz: A car rental company, not an airline. It began in Chicago in the 1910s as a taxi-and-rental firm and is now a staple of airport rental counters.
Airlines.Concorde: A supersonic jet, not an airline. British Airways and Air France both flew it, crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours until 2003.
Airlines.Cessna: A US maker of small propeller planes, not an airline. The Cessna 172 is the most produced aircraft in history, with over 40,000 built.

Add 'ship' to make a word.Friend: Friendship is a bond that research ties to better health, and one famous study even links strong friendships to longer life.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Hard: Hardship comes from hard, and in a nautical twist it has nothing to do with vessels, though it feels like a rough voyage.
Add 'ship' to make a word.War: A warship is a vessel built for combat, and the British HMS Victory, launched in 1765, is the oldest still in commission.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Battle: A battleship was the big-gun giant of naval fleets, and Japan's Yamato, launched in 1940, was the heaviest ever built.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Flag: A flagship carries the commanding admiral, and the term now covers a company's best product or biggest store too.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Space: A spaceship carries crews beyond the atmosphere, and the word is also used for science fiction craft like the Enterprise.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Air: An airship is a lighter-than-air craft like a blimp, and the Hindenburg, at 245 meters, was nearly as long as the Titanic.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Wor: Worship comes from worth plus ship, so it once meant to give something worth, which makes the suffix a state rather than a vessel.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Leader: Leadership means guiding others, and in the suffix sense, ship denotes a quality or state, as in friendship.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Member: Membership is belonging to a group, and the suffix ship here marks a state or condition.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Owner: Ownership means holding legal title to something, and ship in this sense comes from Old English meaning state.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Star: Starship is a science-fiction term popularized by Star Trek, where the USS Enterprise is a famous one.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Steam: A steamship crossed oceans powered by boilers, and the SS Great Western, built in 1838, was a pioneer of Atlantic steam travel.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Court: Courtship is the period of romance before marriage, and in the suffix sense ship marks a state rather than a vessel.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Boat: Boatship isn't a word, though boats and ships are similar, and ship is itself the larger vessel.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Car: Carship isn't a word, and while ships carry cars in roll-on roll-off vessels, we don't join them together.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Train: Trainship isn't a word, though some ferries really did carry railway cars across water.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Bus: Busship isn't a word, and buses ride on roads while ships sail on water.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Plane: Planeship isn't a word, and aircraft are only linked to ships through carrier decks.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Bike: Bikeship isn't a word, though the idea of bikes aboard ships is natural enough.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Truck: Truckship isn't a word, although huge ships carry thousands of trucks as cargo.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Taxi: Taxiship isn't a word, though water taxis do operate in many harbor cities.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Tram: Tramship isn't a word, even though trams and ships both use rails or water as guides.
Add 'ship' to make a word.Van: Vanship isn't a word, though vans are shipped around the globe daily as cargo.

Formula One terms.Pit stop: A top F1 crew changes all four tires in about two seconds, and the record is under two seconds, faster than most people blink twice.
Formula One terms.Pole position: Pole position goes to the driver with the fastest qualifying lap and means starting first on the grid, the best spot.
Formula One terms.Chequered flag: The black-and-white flag waves as the winner crosses the line, and it ends the race for everyone as they finish.
Formula One terms.Pit lane: Pit lane has a strict speed limit, usually 60 or 80 km/h, and breaking it earns a penalty even when cars are only changing tires.
Formula One terms.Safety car: The safety car leads the field slowly after crashes so marshals can clear debris, and it bunches the cars up, often shaking up the race.
Formula One terms.DRS: DRS stands for Drag Reduction System, a flap on the rear wing that opens to help a chasing driver overtake on straights.
Formula One terms.Podium: The top three finishers climb the podium to get trophies and spray champagne, a tradition started in 1967 by Dan Gurney.
Formula One terms.Chicane: A chicane is a tight left-right or right-left kink that forces cars to slow, often added to keep speeds down.
Formula One terms.Pit crew: A pit crew has about 20 people during a stop, with a few on each wheel, one for the jack, and others for the front and rear wings.
Formula One terms.Formation lap: Before the race, cars take a slow warm-up lap to heat tires and brakes and then line up on the grid for the start.
Formula One terms.Touchdown: A touchdown scores six points in American football, so it belongs to a different sport than F1.
Formula One terms.Wicket: In cricket, a wicket is both the three stumps and the dismissal of a batter, and it has no place in motorsport.
Formula One terms.Home run: A home run is a baseball hit over the fence, and Barry Bonds holds the single-season record with 73 in 2001.
Formula One terms.Free throw: Free throws are shot from 15 feet in basketball, and they sit well outside the world of F1.
Formula One terms.Birdie: A birdie in golf is one stroke under par, and the term came from early 1900s slang for something excellent.
Formula One terms.Scrum: A scrum restarts play in rugby, and the forwards bind together and push, which is nothing like racing.
Formula One terms.Checkmate: Checkmate comes from the Persian shah mat, meaning the king is helpless, and it ends a chess game, not a race.
Formula One terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is a basketball shot where a player jams the ball through the hoop from above.
Formula One terms.Bullseye: A bullseye is the center of a dartboard or archery target, and the name may come from a big old English sweet.
Formula One terms.Strike: A strike in bowling means knocking all ten pins down at once, and in baseball it's a missed swing or a pitch in the zone.
Formula One terms.Knockout: A knockout ends a boxing match when a fighter cannot get up in ten seconds, but F1 has no such rule.
Formula One terms.Hole in one: A hole in one is when a golfer sinks the ball with the first shot, and it's very rare for amateurs.
Formula One terms.Penalty corner: A penalty corner is a field hockey set piece, awarded for fouls inside the circle, and it has no F1 counterpart.
Formula One terms.Love-all: In tennis, love means zero, possibly from the French l'oeuf for egg, so love-all is a 0-0 score.

Things on a submarine.Periscope: A periscope lets a submarine see the surface while submerged, and the idea of using mirrors in a tube goes back to the 1800s.
Things on a submarine.Torpedo: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile, and the term comes from the electric ray, whose Latin name was torpedo.
Things on a submarine.Sonar: Sonar stands for sound navigation and ranging, and submarines use it to hear and locate objects through water.
Things on a submarine.Ballast tank: Ballast tanks flood with water to dive and fill with air to surface, which changes the sub's overall buoyancy.
Things on a submarine.Bunk: Submarine crews often practice hot bunking, in which sailors on different shifts share the same bed in turn.
Things on a submarine.Galley: A galley is the ship's kitchen, and good food is crucial for submarine morale on long patrols.
Things on a submarine.Hatch: A hatch is the sealed door through which crew enter, and it has to be watertight to withstand crushing pressure.
Things on a submarine.Control room: The control room is the nerve center where officers steer, dive and operate sonar, and it's also called the conn.
Things on a submarine.Hydrophone: A hydrophone is an underwater microphone that picks up sound, and subs use them to listen for ships and other subs.
Things on a submarine.Crow's nest: A crow's nest is a lookout platform high on a sailing ship's mast, which a submarine doesn't need.
Things on a submarine.Sunroof: A sunroof is a car feature, and a submarine's hull must be sealed tight against water pressure.
Things on a submarine.Landing gear: Landing gear are the wheels of an aircraft, and a submarine doesn't land on anything but water.
Things on a submarine.Chimney: A chimney vents smoke from a fire or furnace, and a sub has no place for open flames.
Things on a submarine.Hot tub: A hot tub is a luxury for spas, and submarines have scarce fresh water, so one aboard is unthinkable.
Things on a submarine.Plank: Walking the plank is a pirate story and a ship thing, not a submarine feature.
Things on a submarine.Diving board: A diving board belongs at a pool, and while a sub dives, it does so by flooding tanks, not by jumping.
Things on a submarine.Jolly Roger: The Jolly Roger is the pirate flag, and yet some British submarines have flown it after returning from successful missions.
Things on a submarine.Hubcap: A hubcap covers a wheel on a car, and a submarine has no wheels.
Things on a submarine.Balcony: A balcony would leak and wreck a submarine's pressure hull, and the vessel is built as a smooth tube.
Things on a submarine.Windsock: A windsock shows wind direction at airfields, and it has no place on a sub that spends most of its time underwater.
Things on a submarine.Paddle wheel: Paddle wheels drove old riverboats, and a submarine moves with propellers, often a single big screw.
Things on a submarine.Treehouse: A treehouse sits among branches, and a submarine is nowhere near a tree.
Things on a submarine.Kickstand: A kickstand props up a bicycle, and a submarine floats in water, so it doesn't need one.
Things on a submarine.Hay bale: Hay bales are farm feed bundles, and they wouldn't be stored inside the tight space of a submarine.

Things you'd find in Venice.Gondola: The traditional boats are painted black under old Venetian rules, and each is built asymmetrically so one oar can steer it straight.
Things you'd find in Venice.Rialto Bridge: The oldest bridge over the Grand Canal, it was finished in 1591 and is lined with shops, and it was long the only crossing.
Things you'd find in Venice.Doge's Palace: This Gothic palace was home to the city's elected rulers, the doges, and it connects to a prison by a covered bridge.
Things you'd find in Venice.Grand Canal: The S-shaped waterway is about 2.5 miles long and is lined with over 170 buildings, mostly from the 1300s to the 1700s.
Things you'd find in Venice.St Mark's Square: Napoleon called it the drawing room of Europe, and its low spot is the first part of Venice to flood in high tides.
Things you'd find in Venice.Murano glass: Glassmakers were moved to the island of Murano in 1291, partly out of fear of fire, and kept their trade secrets closely guarded.
Things you'd find in Venice.Bridge of Sighs: The enclosed bridge linked interrogation rooms to prison cells, and Lord Byron's poem named it for sighs of prisoners.
Things you'd find in Venice.Vaporetto: These water buses are Venice's public transport, running on the canals in place of cars and buses.
Things you'd find in Venice.Lagoon: Venice is built on over a hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon, and its buildings rest on millions of wooden piles.
Things you'd find in Venice.Gondolier: Becoming one takes months of training and an exam, and for most of history the job was handed down within families.
Things you'd find in Venice.Lido: The long island that shields the lagoon is home to the Venice Film Festival, the world's oldest, started in 1932.
Things you'd find in Venice.Colosseum: This amphitheater is in Rome, not Venice, and could seat tens of thousands of spectators almost 2,000 years ago.
Things you'd find in Venice.Trevi Fountain: Rome's biggest Baroque fountain collects about a million euros a year in coins thrown by visitors.
Things you'd find in Venice.Ponte Vecchio: Florence's medieval bridge has jewelers' shops built along it, and it was the only one spared in WWII.
Things you'd find in Venice.Leaning Tower: The tower in Pisa started to lean while it was being built, because its foundations sat on soft ground.
Things you'd find in Venice.Uffizi: Florence's museum began as offices for the Medici family and now holds Botticelli's Birth of Venus.
Things you'd find in Venice.La Scala: Milan's famous opera house opened in 1778, and it is where many of Verdi's operas premiered.
Things you'd find in Venice.Vatican: The world's smallest country sits inside Rome and has its own post office, and a Swiss Guard protects the Pope.
Things you'd find in Venice.Pompeii: The Roman city was buried by Mount Vesuvius in AD 79 and is near Naples, not Venice.
Things you'd find in Venice.Spanish Steps: This famous staircase in Rome has 135 steps, and it's named for a nearby Spanish embassy.
Things you'd find in Venice.Vesuvius: The volcano overlooks the Bay of Naples and is the only active volcano on mainland Europe.
Things you'd find in Venice.Sistine Chapel: Michelangelo painted its ceiling in the early 1500s, and it's inside the Vatican, far from Venice.
Things you'd find in Venice.Mount Etna: Sicily's volcano is one of the world's most active, and it's in the south, far from Venice.
Things you'd find in Venice.Blue Grotto: This sea cave on the island of Capri glows blue when light enters through an underwater opening.

Places to stay overnight on a trip.Hotel: The Hôtel de Ville in French means town hall, since 'hôtel' once meant any grand townhouse before it meant lodging.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Motel: The word fuses 'motor' and 'hotel', and the first, the Milestone Mo-Tel, opened in California in 1925.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Hostel: Hostels began with German teacher Richard Schirrmann, who opened the first ones in the early 1900s for hiking students.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Campsite: Camping became fashionable after a minister's 1869 book, Adventures in the Wilderness, drew crowds into the Adirondacks.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Bed and breakfast: The name states the deal: a room in a private home plus a morning meal, a staple of rural Britain and Ireland.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Inn: Inns date back to Roman times, when imperial roads had them at regular intervals for travelers and horses.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Sleeper train: A sleeper train lets you cross a country while you sleep, saving a night's hotel bill.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Guesthouse: A guesthouse is a small, usually family-run lodging, often cheaper than a hotel and with breakfast included.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Lodge: Ski and hunting lodges are known for their log-cabin looks, and the word comes from the Old French loge, a shelter.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Caravan: A caravan once meant a group of desert travelers, and in Britain it's now a towable mobile home.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Ryokan: A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn with tatami mats, futon bedding and hot-spring baths.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Cafeteria: You eat in a cafeteria, but you don't sleep there; the word comes from Spanish for coffee shop.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Car wash: A car wash cleans cars in a few minutes, so it's a stop, not a stay.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Bank: A bank holds money, not guests, and vault doors are among the few things in town that really lock overnight.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Post office: A post office is for letters and parcels, and in the 1800s some English inns doubled as local mail stops.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Laundromat: The first self-service laundry opened in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1934, as a 'Washateria'.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Pharmacy: A pharmacy dispenses medicine; the word comes from Greek 'pharmakon', which meant both a cure and a poison.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Cinema: A cinema shows films, and though people do fall asleep in one, it isn't lodging.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Library: A library is for reading and quiet; some university ones do stay open all night for students.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Toll booth: A toll booth collects road fees, and long-distance drivers pass through it in the middle of the night.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Bowling alley: A bowling alley is for leisure, and the lanes are oiled for the ball, not for a mattress.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Butcher shop: A butcher shop sells meat, and with its cold rooms would be a chilly place to stay.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Petrol station: A petrol station is a quick stop, and the first ones in the early 1900s were pumps outside shops.
Places to stay overnight on a trip.Dentist: You lie down at a dentist, but only for a filling, not a night.

Things you need a license to drive or fl.Car: In most countries a driver must pass a test, and the first licensing requirements arrived in Germany and France around 1900.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Motorcycle: Motorcycles often need a separate license class, and many places grade it by engine size, with power limits for beginners.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Airplane: Pilots must log many hours of training; to fly an airliner, a pilot needs about 1,500 hours in the United States.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Bus: Bus drivers need a special passenger-carrying license in most countries, because they are responsible for many lives.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Truck: Heavy trucks need a special license, and professional drivers are legally limited in hours to prevent fatigue.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Helicopter: Helicopter pilots need a distinct license, and the machines are famously hard to fly because every control affects another.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Lorry: Lorry is British for truck, and heavy goods vehicles need a special HGV license class in the UK.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Airliner: Airline pilots need an airline transport pilot license, one of the hardest to earn.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Fighter jet: Fighter pilots go through years of selection and training, and may fly at over twice the speed of sound.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Coach: Long-distance coaches require a bus license, and drivers must follow strict limits on driving time.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Bicycle: A trap: you can ride a bike anywhere with no license, which is part of why it is the world's most popular vehicle.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Skateboard: No license is needed for a skateboard, though many cities limit where you can ride it.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Rollerblades: In-line skates need no license, though many riders wear helmets and pads.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Kayak: Kayaks need no license in most places, though some waters require registration for boats of any sort.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Sled: No license is needed for a sled, which is just a gravity-powered fun tool, from child's toy to Olympic bobsled.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Tricycle: Tricycles need no license, and small children ride them long before they can legally drive.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Pogo stick: The pogo stick was invented in the early 1900s, and needs no license to bounce on.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Wheelbarrow: A wheelbarrow, invented in China about 2,000 years ago, needs no license.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Shopping cart: Shopping carts were invented in 1937 in Oklahoma, and no license is needed to push one.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Pram: The pram is short for perambulator, and a parent needs no license to push one.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Unicycle: A unicycle has a single wheel and no license requirement, only a good sense of balance.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Canoe: The word canoe comes from a Caribbean word; no license is needed to paddle one in most places.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Toboggan: The toboggan takes its name from an Algonquian word, and no permit is required for sledding.
Things you need a license to drive or fl.Pedalo: A pedalo is a pedal-powered pleasure boat, and renting one doesn't require a license.

Common pizza toppings.Pepperoni: It's an American invention: in Italy 'peperoni' means bell peppers, while the spicy salami became the favorite US pizza topping.
Common pizza toppings.Mushrooms: Button mushrooms, cremini and portobellos are all the same species, differing mainly in age and color.
Common pizza toppings.Olives: Green and black olives can come from the same tree; the difference is mostly ripeness and how they're cured.
Common pizza toppings.Sausage: Italian sausage is often flavored with fennel seed, which gives pizza its sweet, aromatic edge.
Common pizza toppings.Onions: The oven's heat mellows onions' sharp sulfur compounds and caramelizes their sugars, turning them sweet at the edges.
Common pizza toppings.Bell peppers: Despite the name, they're unrelated to black pepper; green ones are just unripe, and the same fruit turns red.
Common pizza toppings.Basil: The green on a Margherita echoes the Italian flag; legend says the pizza was named for Queen Margherita in 1889.
Common pizza toppings.Mozzarella: Real Neapolitan pizza uses buffalo or cow's milk mozzarella, whose stretched curd gives the famous stringy pull.
Common pizza toppings.Anchovies: Salty and divisive, anchovies melt into the sauce and add umami; Caesar dressing and Worcestershire sauce use them too.
Common pizza toppings.Pineapple: Hawaiian pizza was invented in Canada, not Hawaii, by Greek-born restaurateur Sam Panopoulos in Ontario in the 1960s.
Common pizza toppings.Bacon: It is often partly cooked first, because raw bacon can stay chewy while a pizza crust bakes fast.
Common pizza toppings.Spinach: Popeye is said to have boosted US spinach consumption in the 1930s, though the iron myth was exaggerated.
Common pizza toppings.Marshmallows: Sweet and sticky, they melt into goo; they belong with s'mores and hot cocoa, not savory pizza.
Common pizza toppings.Gummy bears: Hans Riegel of Haribo invented them in Germany in 1922, and in an oven they'd melt into a puddle.
Common pizza toppings.Jam: Fruit preserves belong on toast; sweet-and-savory pizzas may use fig jam, but it is hardly a common topping.
Common pizza toppings.Cornflakes: Invented by the Kellogg brothers in the 1890s as a health food, they would go soggy under tomato sauce.
Common pizza toppings.Chocolate chips: Created at the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts in the 1930s for cookies, they are a sweet, not savory, topping.
Common pizza toppings.Peanut butter: A sandwich spread; Thai-style pizzas sometimes use peanut sauce, but it is not a standard topping.
Common pizza toppings.Whipped cream: It would collapse in an oven; whipped cream is made by trapping air in cream with a fat content of roughly 30 percent or more.
Common pizza toppings.Ice cream: Dessert pizzas exist, but ice cream would melt in the oven, so it can only be added after baking.
Common pizza toppings.Candy corn: This Halloween candy dates to the 1880s; its colored kernel shape suits autumn, not pizza.
Common pizza toppings.Pudding: Pudding is a spoon dessert; sweet custards and savory British puddings exist, but none top pizzas.
Common pizza toppings.Jelly beans: Hard sugar shells keep them candy-sweet on any pizza; Ronald Reagan famously kept jelly beans on his desk.
Common pizza toppings.Oatmeal: Oats are for porridge and cookies; oat flour can make a crust, but oatmeal is not a topping.

Espresso-based drinks.Latte: Italian for 'milk': order just a 'latte' in Italy and you will get a glass of milk.
Espresso-based drinks.Cappuccino: Named for the brown robes of Capuchin friars; in Italy it is traditionally a morning-only drink.
Espresso-based drinks.Americano: Legend says it began when American soldiers in Italy watered down espresso to mimic their drip coffee.
Espresso-based drinks.Macchiato: Means 'stained' in Italian: an espresso marked with just a dash of milk foam.
Espresso-based drinks.Flat white: Australia and New Zealand both claim it; its signature is a silky, velvety microfoam.
Espresso-based drinks.Cortado: Spanish for 'cut': espresso cut with about equal warm milk to soften its acidity.
Espresso-based drinks.Ristretto: A 'restricted' shot pulled with less water, so it is sweeter and more concentrated than regular espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Lungo: Italian for 'long': pulled with more water, giving a larger, more bitter shot than regular espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Mocha: Named for the Yemeni port of Mocha, a historic coffee-trading hub, long before chocolate was added to the drink.
Espresso-based drinks.Doppio: A double espresso, now the standard shot in many cafes.
Espresso-based drinks.Affogato: Means 'drowned': a scoop of ice cream gets drowned in hot espresso, making it a drink and a dessert.
Espresso-based drinks.Red eye: Drip coffee with an espresso shot dropped in, supposedly named for the bleary eyes after a red-eye flight.
Espresso-based drinks.Cold brew: Steeped in cold water for 12 or more hours with no heat or pressure, so it is not espresso-based.
Espresso-based drinks.French press: Coarse grounds steeped in hot water then pressed down by a plunger; no pressure extraction as in espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Pour-over: Hot water dripped through a paper filter by gravity, the slow opposite of espresso's high pressure.
Espresso-based drinks.Turkish coffee: Powder-fine grounds simmered in a small pot; UNESCO lists Turkish coffee culture, but it is not espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Moka pot: Invented by Alfonso Bialetti in 1933, it uses steam pressure well below an espresso machine's, so it is not true espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Instant: Freeze-dried or spray-dried coffee dissolved in hot water, with no pressure involved.
Espresso-based drinks.Aeropress: Invented in 2005 by Alan Adler, who also created the Aerobie flying ring, it makes filter-style coffee, not espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Chai latte: Spiced tea with milk, no coffee at all, despite the word 'latte'.
Espresso-based drinks.Matcha latte: Powdered green tea whisked with milk: a latte in form, but with no espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Hot chocolate: Cocoa and milk with no coffee; Mesoamericans drank a bitter chocolate drink long before sugar and milk arrived.
Espresso-based drinks.Chemex: A glass hourglass-shaped brewer designed in 1941 by chemist Peter Schlumbohm; a filter rig, not espresso.
Espresso-based drinks.Percolator: It cycles boiling water over the grounds again and again, which can over-extract; a classic, but not espresso.

Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).BLT: Its name is just its ingredients' initials, making it one of the few sandwiches known by an abbreviation.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Reuben: Corned beef, Swiss, sauerkraut and Russian dressing on rye; Omaha and New York each claim to have invented it.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Club sandwich: Triple-decker toast pinned with toothpicks, a staple of hotel room service; legend ties its name to a gentlemen's club.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Philly cheesesteak: Credited to hot dog vendor Pat Olivieri in the 1930s, this thin-sliced beef sandwich became a Philadelphia emblem.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Banh mi: The Vietnamese baguette sandwich reflects French colonial heritage, with an airy, thin-crusted loaf.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Croque monsieur: A French grilled ham and cheese; add a fried egg on top and it becomes a croque madame.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Po' boy: A New Orleans sandwich said to have been born in a 1929 streetcar strike to feed the striking 'poor boys'.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Monte Cristo: A ham and cheese sandwich dipped in egg and fried, often dusted with powdered sugar.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Cubano: Ham, roast pork, Swiss, pickles and mustard on pressed Cuban bread; Tampa and Miami argue over whether salami belongs.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Sloppy Joe: Ground beef in tangy sauce on a bun, so messy that the name is a promise.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Muffuletta: A New Orleans Italian sandwich on a round sesame loaf with olive salad, said to have been created at Central Grocery in 1906.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Grilled cheese: Became hugely popular in the United States in the 1920s and 30s with pre-sliced bread and processed cheese.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Burrito: A tortilla wrap, which is exactly what this category excludes; the name means 'little donkey'.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Taco: Filled and folded tortilla, so a wrap-style food, though some argue whether tacos count as sandwiches.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Quesadilla: Cheese in a folded tortilla, a wrap, not a sandwich.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Calzone: Folded pizza dough, from Naples; the name comes from Italian for 'trouser leg'.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Pizza: A flat pie, not two slices of bread; the Neapolitan art of the pizzaiuolo is on UNESCO's heritage list.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Empanada: A baked or fried pastry pocket, named from the Spanish verb for 'wrapped in bread'.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Samosa: A fried triangular pastry whose roots stretch back to Central Asia before it became an Indian snack.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Dumpling: Dough wrapped around filling, a pastry, not a sandwich.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Pasty: The Cornish pasty has protected status in the EU, and legend says its crimped edge gave miners a handle.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Gyoza: Japanese pan-fried dumplings, adapted from Chinese jiaozi.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Spring roll: Wrapped in thin pastry skins and often fried, so a wrap rather than a sandwich.
Named sandwiches (not wraps or pastries).Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, boiled and then often pan-fried, with potato-and-cheese the classic filling.
